simple: Sweating and flushing of the face while eating, from nerves regrowing incorrectly after injury, such as after salivary gland surgery.

name: Guttmann’s Sign
formal: Nasal congestion with facial flushing from autonomic overactivity in acute high spinal cord lesions.
simple: Stuffy nose and facial flushing from overactive nervous system reflexes, seen right after a severe spinal cord injury.

name: Gynaecomastia
formal: Breast enlargement in men; Kennedy disease (SBMA), drugs, endocrine.
simple: Breast tissue enlargement in men, which can be a sign of a rare inherited nerve-muscle disease, certain drugs, or hormone problems.

name: Hallpike Manoeuvre, Hallpike Test
formal: Rapid positioning into head-hanging with head turned; torsional upbeating nystagmus with latency = posterior canal BPPV.
simple: A test where the head is quickly tilted back and turned to one side; if it causes spinning eye movements and dizziness after a short delay, it points to a specific inner-ear cause of vertigo.

name: Hallucination
formal: Perception without an external stimulus (visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory).
simple: Seeing, hearing, feeling, or smelling something that isn't actually there.

name: Hammer Toes
formal: Flexion deformity of the toe IP joints; hereditary neuropathy, Friedreich ataxia.
simple: Toes that are permanently bent at the middle joint, seen in some inherited nerve diseases.

name: Hand Elevation Test
formal: Raising the hands overhead up to 2 min reproduces median paraesthesia; carpal tunnel syndrome.
simple: Holding both arms raised overhead for up to two minutes brings on tingling in the hand, a sign of carpal tunnel syndrome (a pinched wrist nerve).

name: Harlequin Phenomenon, Harlequin Sign, Harlequin Syndrome
formal: Unilateral facial flushing and sweating with the opposite side pale/dry; sympathetic lesion on the pale side.
simple: One side of the face flushes and sweats while the other side stays pale and dry, from a problem in the nerves controlling blood vessels on the pale side.
nN: harlequin phenomenon harlequin sign harlequin syndrome
aN: harlequin phenomenon | harlequin sign | harlequin syndrome

name: Harvey’s Sign
formal: Painful stimulus of a vibrating tuning fork on the nasal septum — arousal response suggests non-organic unresponsiveness.
simple: Touching a painful vibrating tuning fork to the nose causes a response, suggesting a patient who seems unresponsive is not truly unconscious.

name: Head Impulse Test
formal: Rapid small head turn while fixating: corrective catch-up saccade = peripheral vestibular loss on that side (normal in central vertigo).
simple: A quick, small head turn while the patient stares at a fixed point: if the eyes lag and then jerk back to the target, it points to a problem in the inner ear's balance organ on that side.

name: Head Snap
formal: Jerky head movement at the end of finger–nose testing; essential tremor.
simple: A jerky head movement that appears at the end of a finger-to-nose coordination test, seen with essential tremor.

name: Head Tilt
formal: Compensatory head posture, e.g. tilt away from the side of a IV nerve palsy; ocular tilt reaction.
simple: Tilting the head to one side to compensate for an eye muscle problem, such as a weak nerve controlling one eye.

name: Head Turning Sign
formal: Patient turns to the spouse/carer for help when asked questions; cognitive impairment (Alzheimer's disease).
simple: A patient turns to look at their spouse or caregiver for help answering questions, a sign of memory or thinking problems such as Alzheimer's disease.

name: Heautoscopy
formal: Seeing one's double with uncertainty about which is the real self.
simple: The unsettling experience of seeing a double of oneself, unsure which one is really "me."

name: Hemeralopia
formal: Day blindness: poor vision in bright light; cone dystrophy.
simple: Poor vision in bright light or daytime, from a problem in the retina's cone cells.

name: Hemiakinesia
formal: Reduced spontaneous use of one side of the body without weakness; motor neglect.
simple: Using one side of the body less than the other spontaneously, even though there's no actual weakness there; the brain is simply ignoring that side.

name: Hemianomia
formal: Inability to name objects presented to one side (e.g. left hand in callosal disconnection).
simple: Trouble naming objects when they're only shown to one side, for example the left hand, seen when the two halves of the brain can't communicate with each other.

name: Hemiataxia
formal: Unilateral incoordination of limbs; points to an ipsilateral cerebellar or brainstem lesion.
simple: Clumsy, uncoordinated movements limited to one side of the body, from a lesion in the cerebellum or brainstem on the matching side.

name: Hemichorea
formal: Chorea on one side; contralateral basal ganglia lesion, non-ketotic hyperglycemia.
simple: Jerky, dance-like involuntary movements on one side of the body, from a brain lesion on the opposite side, sometimes linked to very high blood sugar.

name: Hemidystonia
formal: Dystonia confined to one side; contralateral putamen/thalamus lesion.
simple: Sustained muscle spasms and abnormal postures limited to one side of the body, from a brain lesion on the opposite side.

name: Hemiparesis
formal: Weakness of one side of the body; contralateral corticospinal lesion.
simple: Weakness of the arm and leg on one side, usually due to damage in the opposite half of the brain.

name: Hemiparkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonism confined to or predominant on one side.
simple: Parkinson's-like symptoms that mainly or only affect one side of the body.

name: Hemiplegia
formal: Complete paralysis of one side of the body.
simple: Complete paralysis of one entire side of the body.

name: Hemiplegia Cruciata
formal: Weakness of one arm and the opposite leg from a lesion at the cervicomedullary junction (pyramidal decussation).
simple: An unusual pattern of weakness in one arm and the opposite leg, from damage at the point where the brain's nerve fibers cross over into the spinal cord.

name: Hemiprosopometamorphopsia
formal: Distorted perception of one half of faces; occipitotemporal or callosal lesion.
simple: Seeing one half of people's faces as distorted, from damage to brain areas that process vision.

name: Hennebert’s Sign
formal: Vertigo/nystagmus provoked by pressure changes in the external ear canal; perilymph fistula, superior canal dehiscence.
simple: Dizziness or eye jerking triggered by pressure changes in the ear canal, seen with certain inner-ear conditions.

name: Henry and Woodruff Sign
formal: Eyes deviate toward the ground whichever side the patient lies on — suggests functional (psychogenic) unresponsiveness.
simple: The eyes always drift toward the ground regardless of which side the patient is lying on, suggesting the unresponsiveness is not from real brain injury but psychological.

name: Heterophoria
formal: Latent ocular deviation controlled by fusion.
simple: A hidden tendency for the eyes to drift out of alignment, normally kept corrected by the brain.

name: Heterotropia
formal: Manifest ocular deviation (squint).
simple: A visible, uncorrected misalignment of the eyes (a squint).

name: Hiccups
formal: Involuntary diaphragmatic myoclonus; persistent hiccups in medullary lesions (e.g. lateral medullary syndrome, NMOSD area postrema).
simple: Involuntary, repeated diaphragm spasms; when persistent, they can signal a lesion in the lower brainstem.

name: Hip Abduction Sign
formal: Thighs abduct when rising from the floor because adductors are weaker than abductors; limb-girdle/proximal myopathy pattern.
simple: When rising from the floor, the thighs spread apart because the inner thigh muscles are weaker than the outer ones, a pattern seen in muscle diseases affecting the hips and shoulders.

name: Hippus
formal: Rhythmic pupil constriction–dilatation; usually normal.
simple: Rhythmic, wave-like widening and narrowing of the pupil, which is usually a normal finding.

name: Hitselberg Sign
formal: Reduced sensation in the posterior external ear canal; vestibular schwannoma (sensory VII fibres).
simple: Reduced feeling in the back of the ear canal, a subtle sign of a tumor on the hearing/balance nerve.

name: Holmes-Adie Pupil, Holmes-Adie Syndrome
formal: Tonic dilated pupil with poor light reaction, slow near response and redilation; with reduced tendon reflexes = Holmes-Adie syndrome.
simple: One pupil is unusually large, reacts poorly to light, and constricts very slowly up close; when combined with reduced reflexes, it's called Holmes-Adie syndrome.

aN: holmes adie pupil | holmes adie syndrome

name: Holmes’ Tremor
formal: Low-frequency rest, postural and intention tremor from midbrain (red nucleus) lesions.
simple: A slow tremor present at rest, when holding a position, and during movement, caused by a lesion deep in the midbrain.

name: Hoover’s Sign
formal: Involuntary hip extension of the "weak" leg when the healthy leg flexes against resistance; functional weakness.
simple: When a patient tries to lift their "weak" leg, it doesn't move, but it presses down involuntarily when the other leg is lifted against resistance — a sign the weakness is functional (not from actual nerve damage).

name: Horologagnosia
formal: Inability to read the time from a clock face with preserved clock setting/numbers.
simple: Inability to tell the time from a clock face, even though the person can still set the clock or knows what the numbers mean.

name: Howship-Romberg Sign
formal: Inner thigh pain from obturator nerve compression, e.g. obturator hernia.
simple: Pain in the inner thigh from a pinched nerve, often caused by a hernia pressing on it near the pelvis.

name: Hoyt-Spencer Sign
formal: Triad of chronic optic nerve compression (e.g. optic nerve sheath meningioma): visual loss, optic disc pallor/swelling and optociliary shunt vessels.
simple: A combination of vision loss, a pale or swollen optic nerve, and abnormal shunt blood vessels on the eye exam, seen with long-standing pressure on the optic nerve from a tumor.

name: Hutchinson’s Pupil
formal: Unilateral dilated unreactive pupil from III nerve compression by uncal herniation.
simple: One pupil becomes large and stops reacting to light because a nerve controlling it is being compressed, often from swelling pushing part of the brain downward.

name: Hyperacusis
formal: Abnormal loudness of sounds; stapedius paralysis (facial palsy), migraine.
simple: Sounds seem abnormally loud, from weakness of a small ear muscle (often with facial nerve palsy) or from migraine.

name: Hyperalgesia
formal: Increased pain response to a painful stimulus.
simple: A painful stimulus causes more pain than it normally would.

name: Hypergraphia
formal: Excessive compulsive writing; temporal lobe epilepsy.
simple: An urge to write excessively, sometimes seen in temporal lobe epilepsy.

name: Hyperhidrosis
formal: Excessive sweating (focal or generalized).
simple: Sweating more than normal, either in specific areas or all over.

name: Hyperkinesia
formal: Excessive involuntary movement.
simple: Too much involuntary movement.

name: Hyperlexia
formal: Precocious ability to read words fluently without understanding them; autism.
simple: Being able to read words fluently at a young age without understanding their meaning, sometimes seen in autism.

name: Hypermetamorphosis
formal: Irresistible urge to notice and respond to each visual stimulus; feature of Klüver–Bucy syndrome.
simple: An uncontrollable urge to notice and react to every single thing seen, part of a rare brain syndrome (Klüver-Bucy syndrome).

name: Hyperorality
formal: Tendency to put objects in the mouth / dietary change; Klüver–Bucy, frontotemporal dementia.
simple: A tendency to put objects in the mouth, or big changes in eating habits, seen in certain brain disorders like frontotemporal dementia.

name: Hyperpathia
formal: Exaggerated, delayed, spreading painful response to stimuli, often with raised threshold; thalamic or nerve lesions.
simple: Pain that is exaggerated, delayed, and spreads out more than expected from the stimulus, often with reduced sensitivity overall; seen with certain brain or nerve lesions.

name: Hyperphagia
formal: Excessive eating; hypothalamic lesions, FTD, Kleine–Levin syndrome.
simple: Eating far more than normal, seen with damage to a brain region (hypothalamus) that controls appetite, or with certain dementias.

name: Hyperphoria
formal: Latent upward deviation of one eye.
simple: A hidden tendency for one eye to drift upward.

name: Hyperpilaphesie
formal: Heightened tactile sensitivity compensating for another sensory loss (e.g. touch in blindness).
simple: An unusually heightened sense of touch that makes up for the loss of another sense, such as vision.

name: Hyperreligiosity
formal: Excessive religious preoccupation; temporal lobe epilepsy, FTD.
simple: Excessive preoccupation with religion, sometimes seen in temporal lobe epilepsy or frontotemporal dementia.

name: Hypersexuality
formal: Increased sexual drive; Klüver–Bucy, dopaminergic drugs, FTD.
simple: An increase in sexual drive or behavior, seen with certain brain disorders or dopamine-related medications.

name: Hyperthermia
formal: Raised body temperature of central origin (hypothalamic/brainstem lesions, NMS).
simple: A raised body temperature caused by a problem in the brain's temperature-control centers, rather than an infection.

name: Hypertonia, Hypertonus
formal: Increased muscle tone (spasticity, rigidity, paratonia).
simple: Increased stiffness or resistance in the muscles.

name: Hypertropia
formal: Manifest upward deviation of one eye; IV nerve palsy, skew deviation.
simple: One eye is visibly turned upward compared to the other.

name: Hypoalgesia
formal: Reduced pain sensation.
simple: Reduced sensitivity to pain.

name: Hypokinesia
formal: Reduced amplitude of movement; parkinsonism.
simple: Movements that are smaller or slower than normal, typical of Parkinson's disease.

name: Hypomimia
formal: Reduced facial expression ("masked face"); parkinsonism.
simple: Reduced facial expression, giving a "mask-like" look, typical of Parkinson's disease.

name: Hypophonia
formal: Soft, quiet voice; parkinsonism.
simple: A soft, quiet voice, typical of Parkinson's disease.

name: Hypophoria
formal: Latent downward deviation of one eye.
simple: A hidden tendency for one eye to drift downward.

name: Hypothermia
formal: Low body temperature of central origin (hypothalamic lesions).
simple: An abnormally low body temperature caused by a problem in the brain's temperature-control centers.

name: Hypotropia
formal: Manifest downward deviation of one eye.
simple: One eye is visibly turned downward compared to the other.

name: Ice Pack Test
formal: Ice applied to a ptotic lid for 2 min improves ptosis in myasthenia gravis.
simple: Placing an ice pack on a drooping eyelid for a couple of minutes and seeing it improve, which supports a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis (a muscle weakness disorder).
th: ประคบน้ำแข็งที่หนังตาตก 2 นาที แล้วหนังตายกขึ้น — สนับสนุน myasthenia gravis
exam: Measure palpebral fissure, apply an ice pack over the closed lid for 2 minutes, re-measure immediately.
pos: Improvement ≥2 mm supports neuromuscular junction ptosis (MG); not useful for ophthalmoparesis or pupil-involving ptosis.

det.mechanism: Cooling reduces acetylcholinesterase activity and may enhance acetylcholine receptor function, prolonging the action of released acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. In myasthenia, this increases the safety margin of transmission, temporarily improving levator strength.
det.technique: Measure the palpebral fissure or margin-reflex distance, then hold an ice pack (wrapped in thin cloth) over the closed ptotic eye for about 2 minutes. Re-measure immediately, as the effect fades within minutes. Compare with a rest test (closed eyes without ice) if needed.
det.interpretation: An improvement of 2 mm or more supports MG with good sensitivity and specificity for ptosis, making it a quick bedside alternative to edrophonium. It is less reliable for diplopia or ophthalmoparesis. A negative test does not exclude MG, and other causes of ptosis (aponeurotic, third nerve, Horner) do not improve.
pearls: Measure immediately after removing the ice.
Useful in emergency departments where antibody results take days.

name: Illusion
formal: Misperception of a real external stimulus.
simple: Misinterpreting something real that is actually there, unlike a hallucination which has no real trigger.

name: Intermanual Conflict
formal: Hands act at cross-purposes; callosal lesions (alien hand).
simple: One hand does something the person didn't intend, as if fighting against the other hand; from damage to the connection between the brain's two halves.

name: Intermetamorphosis
formal: Belief that people have changed into others; misidentification syndrome.
simple: A false belief that people around oneself have transformed into different people.

name: Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO)
formal: Impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye with abducting nystagmus of the other eye; MLF lesion (MS, stroke).
simple: One eye can't turn fully inward while the other eye jerks as it turns outward, from damage to a specific nerve pathway connecting the eye-movement centers; often seen in multiple sclerosis or stroke.
th: ตาข้างหนึ่งหุบเข้าไม่ได้เมื่อมองข้าง ตาอีกข้างกระตุก — รอยโรคที่ MLF ในก้านสมอง
exam: Ask for fast horizontal saccades between two targets; watch the adducting eye for slowness and the abducting eye for nystagmus. Convergence is tested separately.
pos: Slow/limited adduction on the side of the MLF lesion with abducting nystagmus of the other eye; convergence usually preserved. Bilateral in young = MS; unilateral in older = brainstem stroke.
aN: ino | internuclear ophthalmoplegia | mlf syndrome | medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion | adduction lag

det.mechanism: Horizontal gaze is coordinated by the abducens nucleus, which drives the ipsilateral lateral rectus and, via interneurons crossing into the opposite medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus. A lesion of the MLF interrupts this signal, so the eye ipsilateral to the lesion fails to adduct properly on lateral gaze. The abducting eye's nystagmus is thought to reflect adaptive increase in innervation.
det.technique: Ask the patient to make rapid saccades between two targets placed to either side; slowed adduction is the most sensitive finding and may be missed with smooth pursuit only. Watch for dissociated nystagmus in the abducting eye. Test convergence separately — preserved convergence localises to the MLF rather than the medial rectus or third nerve. Check for vertical diplopia, as skew deviation often coexists.
det.interpretation: INO is named for the side of the adduction deficit, which matches the side of the MLF lesion. Bilateral INO in a young adult strongly suggests MS; unilateral INO in an older vascular patient suggests pontine or midbrain infarction. Other causes include Wernicke encephalopathy, trauma and tumour. Myasthenia gravis can mimic INO (pseudo-INO), so consider fatigability and antibody testing.
pearls: Saccades reveal subtle adduction lag better than pursuit.
WEBINO (wall-eyed bilateral INO) suggests a midbrain lesion.
One-and-a-half syndrome = INO + ipsilateral gaze palsy (PPRF or abducens nucleus).
det.thd: INO เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ MLF ในก้านสมองซึ่งส่งสัญญาณจาก abducens nucleus ไปยังกล้ามเนื้อ medial rectus ของตาอีกข้าง ทำให้ตาข้างเดียวกับรอยโรคหุบเข้าช้าหรือไม่สุด และตาอีกข้างกระตุกเมื่อกางออก ตรวจด้วยการกลอกตาเร็วระหว่างเป้าสองข้าง convergence มักปกติ ในคนหนุ่มสาวที่เป็นสองข้างนึกถึง MS ในผู้สูงอายุข้างเดียวนึกถึงหลอดเลือดสมอง และต้องแยก myasthenia

name: Intrusion
formal: Unwanted saccades interrupting fixation, or intrusion errors in memory recall.
simple: Unwanted quick eye movements that interrupt steady focus, or unwanted extra words/ideas that intrude into memory recall.

name: Inverted Reflexes
formal: Tendon tap produces contraction of the antagonist (e.g. inverted supinator jerk → finger flexion) from a root/cord lesion at that level with UMN signs below (e.g. C5–6).
simple: Tapping a tendon causes the opposite muscle group to react instead of the expected one, pointing to a specific level of spinal cord or nerve root damage.

name: Iridoplegia
formal: Paralysis of the iris — pupil fails to react (e.g. III nerve, pharmacological, trauma).
simple: The colored part of the eye (iris) is paralyzed, so the pupil doesn't react properly to light.

name: Jacksonian March
formal: Spread of a focal motor seizure along the homunculus (e.g. hand → arm → face).
simple: A seizure that starts in one small body part and spreads step by step to nearby areas, like from the hand to the arm to the face.

name: Jactitation
formal: Restless tossing about; jerking or restlessness in severe illness.
simple: Restless tossing and turning of the body, often seen in someone who is very sick.

name: Jamais Entendu
formal: Familiar sounds feel unfamiliar; temporal lobe seizure aura.
simple: A familiar sound suddenly feels unfamiliar or strange, sometimes an early warning sign of a temporal lobe seizure.

name: Jamais Vu
formal: Familiar surroundings feel strange/unfamiliar; temporal lobe seizure aura.
simple: Familiar surroundings suddenly feel strange or unfamiliar, sometimes an early warning sign of a temporal lobe seizure.

name: Jaw Winking
formal: Marcus Gunn phenomenon: ptotic eyelid elevates with jaw opening/lateral movement; congenital trigemino-oculomotor synkinesis.
simple: A drooping eyelid lifts up automatically when the jaw opens or moves sideways, from miswired nerves present from birth.

name: Jendrassik’s Manoeuvre
formal: Reinforcement: pulling hooked fingers apart (or clenching teeth) to bring out a tendon reflex that seems absent.
simple: Having the patient pull their own hooked fingers apart or clench their teeth to help bring out a tendon reflex that otherwise seems absent.

name: Jitteriness
formal: Exaggerated startle / tremulousness, especially in neonates; must be distinguished from clonic seizures.
simple: Exaggerated startling or trembling, especially in newborns, which needs to be told apart from actual seizures.

name: Jugular Foramen Syndrome
formal: Ipsilateral IX, X, XI palsies (Vernet syndrome): dysphagia, dysphonia, weak SCM/trapezius.
simple: Weakness of several nerves on one side of the throat and neck together, causing swallowing trouble, voice changes, and weak shoulder/neck muscles.

name: Kayser-Fleischer Rings
formal: Golden-brown corneal ring from copper deposition; Wilson disease.
simple: A golden-brown ring around the edge of the cornea from copper buildup, a sign of Wilson disease (a genetic copper disorder).

name: Kernohan’s Notch Syndrome
formal: Hemiparesis ipsilateral to a supratentorial mass from compression of the opposite cerebral peduncle; false-localizing.
simple: Weakness on the same side as a brain mass, which is unusual and misleading, because the mass is actually pressing on the opposite side of the brain.

name: Kinesis Paradoxica
formal: Sudden, surprisingly fast effective movement in a parkinsonian patient under emotional stress or with cues.
simple: A person with Parkinson's disease suddenly moves quickly and normally during an emotional moment or when given a specific cue, despite usual slowness.

name: Klazomania
formal: Compulsive shouting (vocal tics), originally post-encephalitic.
simple: Uncontrollable, compulsive shouting, historically linked to a viral brain infection.

name: Kleptomania
formal: Compulsive stealing; frontotemporal dementia, compulsive disorders.
simple: An uncontrollable urge to steal, seen in some dementias and impulse-control disorders.

name: Klüver-Bucy Syndrome
formal: Hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity, visual agnosia and hypermetamorphosis; bilateral anterior temporal lesions (HSV encephalitis, FTD).
simple: A rare combination of overeating or mouthing objects, increased sexual behavior, unusual calmness, trouble recognizing objects visually, and reacting to every stimulus; from damage to both temporal lobes of the brain.

name: Knee Bobbing, Knee Tremor
formal: Rapid knee "bobbing" on standing; primary orthostatic tremor (13–18 Hz).
simple: Fast, rhythmic knee shaking that appears only while standing still, a sign of a rare tremor disorder affecting balance while standing.

name: Korber-Salus-Elschnig Syndrome
formal: Convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze; dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome.
simple: The eyes jerk and pull inward together when trying to look upward, part of a syndrome from damage to the back of the midbrain.

name: Kyphoscoliosis
formal: Combined forward and lateral spinal curvature; neuromuscular disease, Friedreich ataxia.
simple: The spine curves both forward and sideways at the same time, seen in some muscle and nerve diseases.

name: Lagophthalmos
formal: Incomplete eyelid closure; facial (orbicularis) weakness.
simple: The eyelid can't close all the way, from weakness of the facial muscles.

name: Lambert’s Sign
formal: Grip strength increases over a few seconds of sustained effort; Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
simple: Grip strength gets stronger the longer someone squeezes, an unusual finding in a nerve-muscle disorder called Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

name: Lasègue’s Sign
formal: Raising the straight leg reproduces radicular pain at 30–70°; L5/S1 radiculopathy.
simple: Lifting a straightened leg brings on shooting leg pain at a certain angle, suggesting a pinched nerve root in the lower back.

name: Laterocollis
formal: Lateral tilt of the head toward the shoulder; cervical dystonia.
simple: The head tilts sideways toward one shoulder, from involuntary neck muscle spasms.

name: Lateropulsion
formal: Involuntary falling/leaning to one side; lateral medullary syndrome, thalamic/vestibular lesions.
simple: An involuntary pull or lean toward one side while sitting, standing, or walking, from damage to the brainstem, thalamus, or balance system.

name: Leucocoria
formal: White pupillary reflex instead of red; retinoblastoma, cataract, retinal detachment.
simple: The pupil looks white instead of red in photos or under light, which can be a sign of a serious eye tumor or cataract in children and needs urgent evaluation.

name: Levitation
formal: Spontaneous rising of an alien limb; parietal lesions, corticobasal degeneration.
simple: An arm or leg that doesn't feel like it belongs to the person rises up on its own, from damage to a brain region called the parietal lobe.

name: Lhermitte’s Sign
formal: Electric-shock sensation down the spine/limbs on neck flexion; cervical cord lesion (MS, B12, compression, radiation).
simple: An electric-shock-like sensation shooting down the spine or limbs when bending the neck forward, from irritation of the spinal cord in the neck, often in multiple sclerosis.
th: ก้มคอแล้วรู้สึกไฟช็อตลงหลังหรือแขนขา — รอยโรคไขสันหลังส่วนคอบริเวณ dorsal column
exam: Ask the patient to flex the neck fully, chin to chest; ask about electric sensations.
pos: Brief electric shocks down the spine/limbs = cervical dorsal column lesion (MS, B12 deficiency, cervical spondylosis, radiation).
aN: lhermitte | barber chair sign | electric shock on neck flexion

det.mechanism: Demyelinated or damaged axons in the cervical dorsal columns become mechanosensitive. Neck flexion stretches the cervical cord, and these hyperexcitable fibres generate ectopic bursts of impulses perceived as electric sensations radiating along the spine or into the limbs.
det.technique: Ask whether bending the head forward causes an electric or buzzing sensation; this symptom is usually reported spontaneously. On examination, passive or active full neck flexion may reproduce it. The sensation is brief and stops when the neck straightens.
det.interpretation: Lhermitte's phenomenon indicates a cervical cord lesion involving the dorsal columns; MS is the classic cause, but cervical spondylotic myelopathy, B12 or nitrous oxide-related myelopathy, radiation myelopathy, cervical tumour and cisplatin toxicity also produce it. It is not specific for MS. A reverse Lhermitte (triggered by neck extension) suggests cervical spondylosis.
pearls: A symptom more than a sign — ask about it directly.
Ask about nitrous oxide use in young people with Lhermitte and sensory ataxia.
det.thd: Lhermitte คือความรู้สึกเหมือนไฟช็อตวิ่งลงหลังหรือแขนขาเมื่อก้มคอ เกิดเพราะใยประสาทใน dorsal column ของไขสันหลังส่วนคอที่เสียหายไวต่อการยืด มักได้จากการซักประวัติ สาเหตุคลาสสิกคือ MS แต่ยังพบใน B12 ต่ำ การใช้ไนตรัสออกไซด์ กระดูกคอกดทับ และหลังฉายรังสี จึงไม่จำเพาะต่อ MS

name: Lid Retraction
formal: Upper lid elevated exposing sclera above the cornea; thyroid eye disease, dorsal midbrain (Collier sign).
simple: The upper eyelid sits too high, showing white above the colored part of the eye, seen in thyroid eye disease or certain brainstem lesions.

name: Locked-in Syndrome
formal: Quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements/blinking; ventral pontine lesion.
simple: A person is fully paralyzed and unable to speak but remains fully awake and aware, usually still able to move their eyes up and down and blink; from a lesion in the front part of the brainstem.

name: Logoclonia
formal: Repetition of the final syllable of words; reiterative speech disorder, advanced Alzheimer's/parkinsonism.
simple: Repeating the last part of a word over and over while speaking, seen in advanced Alzheimer's disease or Parkinson's disease.

name: Logopenia
formal: Reduced speech output with word-finding pauses and impaired repetition; logopenic variant primary progressive aphasia.
simple: Speech that comes out slower with frequent pauses to find words, along with trouble repeating phrases; a pattern seen in a specific type of progressive language decline.

name: Logorrhoea
formal: Excessive, often incoherent talking; Wernicke aphasia, mania, frontal lesions.
simple: Talking excessively and often making little sense; seen with certain language problems after brain damage, mania, or frontal brain injury.

name: Lower Motor Neurone (LMN) Syndrome
formal: Weakness with wasting, fasciculation, hypotonia and reduced/absent reflexes.
simple: Weak, wasted, twitchy muscles with reduced reflexes, from damage to the nerve cells that connect directly to muscles.

name: Macropsia
formal: Objects appear smaller than they are; macular or cortical causes, migraine.
simple: Things look smaller than they really are; caused by eye (macula) problems, certain brain lesions, or migraine.

name: Maculopathy
formal: Disease of the macula causing central visual loss and metamorphopsia.
simple: A disease of the central part of the retina (macula) that blurs central vision and can make straight lines look wavy.

name: Magnetic Movements
formal: Limb follows the examiner's touch as if magnetised (e.g. foot follows hand); frontal lobe dysfunction.
simple: The limb seems drawn to follow the examiner's hand, as if magnetized; seen with frontal lobe brain problems.

name: Main d’Accoucheur
formal: Carpopedal spasm posture (wrist flexion, MCP flexion, fingers extended/adducted); tetany from hypocalcaemia.
simple: A hand posture with the wrist bent and fingers drawn together, seen in muscle spasms from low blood calcium.

name: Main Succulente
formal: Swollen, cyanotic hand with thickened skin and trophic changes; syringomyelia.
simple: A swollen, bluish, thick-skinned hand with skin changes; seen with a spinal cord condition called syringomyelia.

name: Malapropisms
formal: Substitution of a similar-sounding but wrong word; paraphasic error.
simple: Using a wrong word that sounds like the right one by mistake, a type of speech error seen in some language disorders.

name: Man-in-the-Barrel
formal: Bilateral arm weakness with preserved leg strength; bilateral watershed infarcts, central cord lesions, ALS (flail arm).
simple: Weakness in both arms while the legs stay strong, as if arms are stuck in a barrel; from certain stroke patterns or nerve disease.

name: Marche à Petit Pas
formal: Short-stepped shuffling gait with upright posture; small vessel disease (vascular parkinsonism).
simple: Walking with small, shuffling steps while staying upright; typical of small blood vessel disease in the brain.

name: Mask-Like Facies
formal: Expressionless face (hypomimia); parkinsonism.
simple: A blank, unmoving facial expression with little blinking; a hallmark of Parkinson's disease.

name: Masseter Hypertrophy
formal: Enlarged masseter muscles; bruxism, oromandibular dystonia.
simple: Enlarged jaw muscles, usually from teeth grinding or a jaw movement disorder.

name: McArdle’s Sign
formal: Leg weakness and stiffness increase with neck flexion (compared with neck extension); cervical cord (MS) lesion.
simple: Leg stiffness and weakness get worse when the neck is bent forward; suggests a problem in the neck part of the spinal cord.

name: Medial Medullary Syndrome
formal: Ipsilateral XII palsy with contralateral hemiparesis and loss of proprioception; anterior spinal / vertebral artery occlusion.
simple: A brainstem stroke giving weakness of half the tongue, with weakness and loss of position sense in the limbs of the other side.

name: Menace Reflex
formal: Blink to a sudden threatening hand movement toward the eye; tests visual fields in uncooperative patients.
simple: Blinking in response to a hand suddenly moving toward the eye; used to check vision in patients who cannot cooperate with formal testing.

name: Metamorphopsia
formal: Distortion of shape/size of seen objects; macular or occipital/parietal lesions.
simple: Objects look distorted in shape or size; from problems in the retina or the brain's vision areas.

name: Micrographia
formal: Small handwriting that becomes smaller as writing continues; Parkinson's disease.
simple: Handwriting that is small and keeps shrinking as someone writes; common in Parkinson's disease.

name: Milkmaid’s Grip
formal: Rhythmic squeezing and relaxing when gripping the examiner's fingers (motor impersistence); chorea.
simple: An inability to hold a steady handshake grip, with the hand squeezing and relaxing rhythmically instead; seen in chorea, a jerky movement disorder.

name: Minimally Conscious State
formal: Severely altered consciousness with minimal but definite, inconsistent evidence of awareness (e.g. visual tracking, following commands).
simple: A severe consciousness disorder where a person shows occasional, inconsistent signs of awareness, like following a simple command.

name: Miosis
formal: Small pupil; Horner syndrome, opioids, pontine lesions, age.
simple: An abnormally small pupil, seen with certain nerve problems, opioid drugs, or simply aging.

name: Mirror Agnosia, Mirror Apraxia, Mirror Ataxia
formal: Reaching into the mirror instead of toward the real object seen in it; parietal lesions.
simple: Reaching toward an object's reflection in a mirror instead of the real object; caused by damage to a brain area handling spatial awareness.
nN: mirror agnosia mirror apraxia mirror ataxia
aN: mirror agnosia | mirror apraxia | mirror ataxia

name: Mirror Sign
formal: Failure to recognise one's own reflection in a mirror, treating it as another person; dementia (misidentification).
simple: Not recognizing one's own reflection and thinking it is another person; seen in some forms of dementia.

name: Mirror Writing
formal: Writing that is reversed as in a mirror; left-handers, hemispheric lesions.
simple: Writing that comes out backwards, as if reflected in a mirror; can occur in some left-handed people or after certain brain injuries.

name: Misidentification Syndromes
formal: Delusional misidentification: Capgras, Fregoli, intermetamorphosis, reduplicative paramnesia.
simple: A group of conditions where someone wrongly believes people, places, or things have been replaced or altered, such as thinking a loved one is an impostor.

name: Misophonia
formal: Strong negative emotional reaction to specific everyday sounds (chewing, breathing).
simple: A strong, uncomfortable emotional reaction to ordinary sounds like chewing or breathing.

name: Misoplegia
formal: Hatred of a paralysed limb; right hemisphere lesions.
simple: Feeling hatred toward one's own paralyzed limb, seen after certain right-sided brain injuries.

name: Mitmachen
formal: Patient allows every passive movement then returns the part to rest when released; frontal dysfunction/catatonia.
simple: The patient passively lets an examiner move their limb into any position and does not resist; seen with frontal brain problems or catatonia.

name: Monoballismus
formal: Ballistic flinging movements of one limb; contralateral subthalamic lesion.
simple: Sudden, large flinging movements in just one limb, from a problem in a small deep brain structure on the opposite side.

name: Monochromatopsia
formal: Complete colour blindness — only one colour/greyscale is seen.
simple: Complete color blindness, seeing everything in shades of one color or gray.

name: Monoparesis, Monoplegia
formal: Weakness or paralysis of one limb; cortical, root, plexus or nerve lesion.
simple: Weakness or complete paralysis limited to a single limb.

name: Monotonia
formal: Restricted pitch/inflection of speech (monotone); hypokinetic dysarthria in parkinsonism.
simple: Speech that sounds flat with little variation in pitch, common in Parkinson's disease.

name: Moria
formal: Inappropriate, silly jocularity; frontal lobe lesions (overlaps with Witzelsucht).
simple: Silly, inappropriate joking that doesn't fit the situation; seen with frontal lobe brain damage.

name: Motor Neglect
formal: Underuse of one side despite normal strength that improves with encouragement; contralateral hemisphere lesion.
simple: Not using one side of the body as much even though it is not truly weak, and using it more when reminded; from damage to one side of the brain.

name: Moving Ear
formal: Rhythmic involuntary ear movement — focal myoclonus/dyskinesia of auricular muscles.
simple: Involuntary rhythmic twitching of the ear muscles.

name: Mutism
formal: Absence of speech; akinetic mutism, severe aphasia, catatonia, functional.
simple: A complete absence of speech, which can occur with severe brain injury, aphasia, catatonia, or psychological causes.

name: Myasthenic Snarl
formal: Transverse, horizontal smile from weak levator anguli oris; myasthenia gravis.
simple: A flat, horizontal smile instead of a normal curved one, because the muscle that lifts the corner of the mouth is weak; seen in myasthenia gravis.

name: Mydriasis
formal: Dilated pupil; III nerve palsy, Adie pupil, pharmacological, trauma.
simple: An abnormally large, dilated pupil, from nerve damage, certain drugs, injury, or a condition called Adie pupil.

name: Myelopathy
formal: Spinal cord dysfunction: UMN signs, sensory level, sphincter disturbance.
simple: A general term for spinal cord damage causing stiffness, weakness, numbness below the injury, and bladder or bowel problems.

name: Myoedema
formal: Localised muscle mounding after percussion (electrically silent); hypothyroidism, rippling muscle disease.
simple: A local muscle bulge that appears after tapping the muscle and fades slowly; seen with an underactive thyroid or certain muscle diseases.

name: Myokymia
formal: Continuous, undulating "bag of worms" muscle rippling; facial myokymia (MS, pontine glioma), radiation plexopathy, neuromyotonia.
simple: Continuous, rippling muscle twitching that looks like worms moving under the skin; seen in some brain, nerve, or radiation-related conditions.

name: Myopathy
formal: Primary muscle disease: usually proximal symmetric weakness with preserved sensation and reflexes.
simple: A disease of the muscles themselves, usually causing weakness closest to the trunk (shoulders and hips) while feeling and reflexes stay normal.

name: Myotonia
formal: Delayed muscle relaxation after contraction (grip) or percussion; myotonic dystrophy, myotonia congenita.
simple: Muscles that stay contracted too long and relax slowly after gripping something or being tapped; seen in certain inherited muscle diseases.

name: Negativism
formal: Resistance to instructions or doing the opposite; catatonia.
simple: Opposing or doing the reverse of instructions; a feature of catatonia.

name: Negro’s Sign
formal: Cogwheel (jerky) rigidity in parkinsonism; also increased eye elevation on the side of a facial palsy on upgaze.
simple: A jerky, ratchet-like stiffness in Parkinson's disease, or extra eye movement on the side of a facial weakness when looking up.

name: Neologism
formal: Non-existent word produced in speech; fluent (Wernicke/jargon) aphasia.
simple: Making up a nonsense word while speaking; seen in a type of language disorder called fluent aphasia.

name: Nerve Thickening
formal: Palpably enlarged peripheral nerves (greater auricular, ulnar, common peroneal); leprosy, CIDP, hereditary demyelinating neuropathy, amyloid.
simple: Peripheral nerves that can be felt as abnormally thick under the skin; seen in leprosy and certain inherited or inflammatory nerve diseases.

name: Neuromyotonia
formal: Continuous muscle fibre activity: myokymia, cramps, pseudomyotonia, hyperhidrosis; Isaacs syndrome (anti-CASPR2).
simple: Constant, uncontrolled muscle nerve activity causing rippling, cramps, and sweating; often from an autoimmune condition called Isaacs syndrome.

name: Neuronopathy
formal: Peripheral nerve disease: distal sensory loss, weakness, reduced reflexes.
simple: A disease affecting peripheral nerves, causing numbness, weakness, and weak reflexes, usually worse in the hands and feet.

name: Nuchocephalic Reflex
formal: Normal adults blink when the shoulders are turned rapidly with eyes closed; persistence of head turning with shoulders suggests diffuse cerebral dysfunction.
simple: Normally, closing the eyes and turning the shoulders makes the head lag behind; if the head instead keeps turning with the shoulders, it suggests widespread brain dysfunction.

name: Obtundation
formal: Reduced alertness with slowed responses; between drowsiness and stupor.
simple: A state of reduced alertness with slow responses, less severe than a coma but more than simple drowsiness.

name: Ocular Apraxia
formal: Difficulty initiating voluntary saccades with head thrusts to compensate; Balint syndrome, congenital, ataxia-telangiectasia.
simple: Trouble voluntarily aiming the eyes toward a target, so the person moves their whole head instead; seen in certain brain and genetic conditions.

name: Ocular Bobbing
formal: Fast downward jerk of both eyes then slow return; pontine lesion (coma).
simple: Both eyes jerk quickly downward then drift slowly back up; seen in comatose patients with brainstem damage.

name: Ocular Dipping
formal: Slow downward eye movement then fast return (reverse of bobbing); diffuse anoxic injury.
simple: Eyes drift slowly downward then snap quickly back up, the reverse pattern of ocular bobbing; seen after widespread lack of oxygen to the brain.

name: Ocular Flutter
formal: Back-to-back horizontal saccades without intersaccadic interval; cerebellar/brainstem disorders.
simple: Rapid back-to-back horizontal eye jerks with no pause between them; seen with cerebellar or brainstem disorders.

name: Oculocephalic Response
formal: Eye movement opposite to passive head turning (doll's eyes); intact brainstem in coma.
simple: In an unconscious patient, turning the head causes the eyes to move in the opposite direction, like doll's eyes; shows the brainstem is working.

name: Oculogyric Crisis
formal: Tonic, usually upward, eye deviation lasting minutes-hours; drug-induced (neuroleptics), post-encephalitic.
simple: Both eyes get stuck looking upward for minutes to hours; a reaction to certain antipsychotic drugs or past brain infection.

name: Oculomotor (III) Nerve Palsy
formal: Ptosis, eye "down and out", ± dilated pupil; pupil-involving = compressive (e.g. PComm aneurysm) until proven otherwise.
simple: A drooping eyelid with the eye pointing down and out, sometimes with a dilated pupil; if the pupil is affected, it may signal a dangerous compressing aneurysm.

name: Ophthalmoparesis, Ophthalmoplegia
formal: Weakness or paralysis of eye movements (nerve, NMJ, muscle or supranuclear).
simple: Partial or complete weakness of eye movements, from a problem anywhere between the nerve and the eye muscle.

name: Opisthotonos
formal: Arched back with head and heels bent backward; tetanus, meningism, dystonic crisis, functional.
simple: The back arches backward with the head and heels curling back; seen in tetanus, severe muscle spasm, or meningitis.

name: Oppenheim’s Sign
formal: Firm downward stroking along the tibia produces an extensor plantar response; corticospinal lesion.
simple: Firmly stroking down the shin causes the big toe to point upward, similar to the classic Babinski reflex; suggests damage to the brain's motor pathway.

name: Opsoclonus
formal: Chaotic multidirectional back-to-back saccades; paraneoplastic (neuroblastoma, breast/lung cancer), post-infectious.
simple: Rapid, chaotic eye movements in all directions with no pause; can be a sign of cancer elsewhere in the body or a past infection.

name: Optic Aphasia
formal: Inability to name visually presented objects despite recognising them (can mime use); left occipital + splenium lesions.
simple: Being unable to name an object you can see, even though you clearly recognize what it is and can show how to use it; from a specific brain lesion affecting vision and language.

name: Optic Atrophy
formal: Pale optic disc from loss of optic nerve fibres (end-stage of many optic neuropathies).
simple: A pale-looking optic nerve seen on eye exam, meaning the nerve fibers carrying vision have been damaged, usually from an earlier condition.

name: Orofacial Dyspraxia
formal: Inability to perform learned face/mouth movements on command (blow, lick lips); left frontal/insular lesions.
simple: Trouble performing learned mouth and face movements on command, like blowing a kiss, despite the muscles themselves working fine.

name: Oromandibular Dystonia
formal: Dystonia of jaw, lips and tongue (jaw opening/closing, deviation); idiopathic, tardive, MSA.
simple: Involuntary muscle spasms of the jaw, lips, and tongue causing abnormal jaw opening, closing, or twisting.

name: Orthostatic Hypotension
formal: Fall in BP ≥20/10 mmHg within 3 min of standing; autonomic failure (MSA, PD, neuropathy), drugs.
simple: A drop in blood pressure upon standing up, often causing dizziness; from a nervous system that fails to adjust blood pressure properly, or from medications.

name: Oscillopsia
formal: Illusion that the environment is moving/oscillating; acquired nystagmus, bilateral vestibular loss.
simple: A false sense that the surroundings are shaking or moving, usually from abnormal eye movements or inner-ear balance problems.

name: Oscillucusis
formal: Perceived oscillation in the loudness of ambient sounds; migraine.
simple: Sounds seeming to get louder and quieter in a wave-like pattern; associated with migraine.

name: Osculation
formal: Kissing behaviour from disinhibition; frontotemporal dementia.
simple: Inappropriate kissing behavior from a loss of normal social inhibition, seen in a type of dementia affecting the frontal and temporal lobes.

name: Osmophobia
formal: Aversion to odours during headache; supports migraine.
simple: A strong dislike of smells during a headache, which supports a diagnosis of migraine.

name: Palilalia
formal: Involuntary repetition of one's own words/phrases with increasing speed; parkinsonism, PSP.
simple: Repeating one's own words or phrases over and over, getting faster each time; seen in Parkinson's disease and related conditions.

name: Palinacousis, Palinacusis
formal: Persistence or recurrence of heard sounds after the stimulus ends; temporal lobe lesions.
simple: Continuing to hear a sound, or hearing it again, after it has actually stopped; from a problem in the brain's temporal lobe.

name: Palinopsia
formal: Persistence or recurrence of visual images after the stimulus is removed; occipitoparietal lesions, drugs, migraine.
simple: Continuing to see an image, or seeing it reappear, after it is no longer actually there; from certain brain lesions, drugs, or migraine.

name: Palmaris Brevis Sign
formal: Preserved palmaris brevis contraction (skin wrinkling on hypothenar) with ulnar-innervated hand weakness localises the lesion to the deep branch in Guyon's canal.
simple: A small muscle in the hand still works even though other ulnar-nerve muscles are weak, which helps pinpoint exactly where along the nerve the damage is.

name: Paradoxical Abdominal Wall Movement, Paradoxical Breathing
formal: Abdomen moves inward on inspiration (abdominal paradox); diaphragmatic weakness (ALS, myopathy, neuropathy).
simple: The belly caves in instead of pushing out when breathing in; a sign the diaphragm (main breathing muscle) is weak.
nN: paradoxical abdominal wall movement paradoxical breathing
aN: paradoxical abdominal wall movement | paradoxical breathing

name: Paraesthesia
formal: Abnormal spontaneous sensation (pins and needles, tingling).
simple: An abnormal sensation like tingling, pins and needles, without anything actually touching the skin.

name: Parakinesia, Parakinesis
formal: Chorea blended into semi-purposeful movements to disguise it.
simple: Hiding involuntary jerky movements by blending them into normal-looking, purposeful actions.

name: Paralysis
formal: Complete loss of voluntary movement.
simple: A complete inability to move a body part voluntarily.

name: Paramnesia
formal: Distorted memory or confusion of fact and fantasy (e.g. déjà vu, reduplicative paramnesia).
simple: Confused or distorted memories, such as a false sense of familiarity (deja vu) or believing a place has been duplicated.

name: Paraparesis
formal: Weakness of both legs; spinal cord, parasagittal or cauda equina lesions, neuropathy.
simple: Weakness affecting both legs, from a problem in the spinal cord, nerves, or nerve roots.

name: Paraphasia
formal: Wrong word (semantic) or wrong sound (phonemic) substitutions in speech; aphasia.
simple: Saying the wrong word or the wrong sounds within a word while speaking; a feature of language disorders called aphasia.

name: Paraplegia
formal: Complete paralysis of both legs.
simple: Complete paralysis of both legs.

name: Parapraxia, Parapraxis
formal: Errors in performing skilled acts (apraxic errors), not merely "Freudian slips".
simple: Mistakes made while trying to perform a skilled physical action, not simply a verbal slip of the tongue.

name: Paresis
formal: Partial weakness.
simple: Partial weakness of a muscle or limb, less severe than full paralysis.

name: Parinaud’s Syndrome
formal: Dorsal midbrain syndrome: upgaze palsy, light–near dissociation, convergence–retraction nystagmus, lid retraction.
simple: A cluster of eye findings from damage deep in the midbrain: trouble looking up, unusual pupil reactions, and abnormal eye-twitching when trying to look up.

name: Parosmia
formal: Distorted smell perception.
simple: A distorted sense of smell, where things smell different than they should.

name: Parry-Romberg Syndrome
formal: Progressive hemifacial atrophy of skin, fat, muscle and bone, sometimes with ipsilateral brain lesions and seizures.
simple: Gradual shrinking of the skin, fat, muscle, and sometimes bone on one side of the face, occasionally with related brain issues or seizures.

name: Peduncular Hallucinosis
formal: Vivid, naturalistic visual hallucinations with brainstem signs; midbrain/thalamic lesions.
simple: Vivid, realistic visual hallucinations occurring alongside other brainstem symptoms, from damage to the midbrain or thalamus.

name: Peek Sign
formal: On sustained gentle eye closure the orbicularis fatigues and the palpebral fissure opens ("peeks"); myasthenia gravis.
simple: When someone holds their eyes gently closed, the eyelids gradually open on their own from muscle fatigue; a sign of myasthenia gravis.

name: Peliopsia
formal: Objects appear nearer than they are.
simple: Objects appearing closer than they truly are.

name: Pelvic Thrusting
formal: Pelvic thrusting movements during seizures; frontal lobe epilepsy or functional (dissociative) seizures.
simple: Pelvic thrusting movements that can occur during a seizure, whether from actual epilepsy or a stress-related seizure-like episode.

name: Pendular Nystagmus
formal: Sinusoidal nystagmus without fast phase; MS, oculopalatal tremor, congenital, visual loss.
simple: A smooth, back-and-forth eye wobble with no quick correcting jerk; seen with multiple sclerosis, poor vision, or from birth.

name: Percussion Myotonia
formal: Sustained dimple/contraction after percussion of a muscle (thenar, tongue); myotonic disorders.
simple: Tapping a muscle causes it to dimple and stay contracted briefly instead of relaxing normally; a sign of certain inherited muscle diseases.

name: Periodic Respiration
formal: Waxing–waning breathing (Cheyne–Stokes); bilateral hemispheric/diencephalic dysfunction, heart failure.
simple: Breathing that gradually gets deeper then shallower in a repeating cycle; from brain dysfunction or heart failure.

name: Perseveration
formal: Inappropriate repetition of a previous response or action; frontal lobe dysfunction.
simple: Getting stuck repeating a word, action, or answer inappropriately; a sign of frontal lobe brain trouble.

name: Personification of Paralysed Limbs
formal: Giving the paralysed limb a name or personality; right hemisphere stroke, often after anosognosia.
simple: Giving a paralyzed limb its own name or personality, often seen after a right-sided stroke along with denial of the paralysis.

name: Pes Cavus
formal: High-arched foot; hereditary neuropathy (CMT), Friedreich ataxia, spinal dysraphism.
simple: A foot with an unusually high arch, often linked to inherited nerve diseases affecting the legs.

name: Phantom Chromatopsia
formal: Perception of colours without a stimulus (e.g. after optic neuritis).
simple: Seeing colors that aren't really there, sometimes after an episode of optic nerve inflammation.

name: Phantom Limb
formal: Persistent sensation (± pain) of an amputated limb.
simple: Ongoing sensations, sometimes painful, that feel like they're coming from a limb that has been amputated.

name: Phantom Vision
formal: Visual perceptions in a blind field or after enucleation.
simple: Seeing images in a part of the visual field that is actually blind, or after an eye has been removed.

name: Phantosmia
formal: Olfactory hallucination (smelling odours that are not present); epilepsy, PD, post-viral.
simple: Smelling an odor that isn't actually present; can occur with epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, or after a viral illness.

name: Phonagnosia
formal: Inability to recognise familiar voices; right temporoparietal lesions.
simple: Trouble recognizing people by their voice alone, from damage to a specific brain area.

name: Phonemic Disintegration
formal: Distorted, inconsistent speech sound errors; apraxia of speech.
simple: Speech sounds that come out garbled and inconsistent; a feature of a speech-planning disorder.

name: Photism
formal: Visual sensation induced by a non-visual stimulus (e.g. sound).
simple: Experiencing a visual sensation triggered by something non-visual, such as seeing colors when hearing a sound.

name: Photophobia
formal: Discomfort/pain from light; migraine, meningitis, SAH, anterior uveitis.
simple: Discomfort or pain in the eyes from bright light, common with migraine, meningitis, or eye inflammation.

name: Photopsia
formal: Flashes of light; retinal detachment/traction, migraine aura, occipital seizures.
simple: Seeing brief flashes of light, which can signal a retinal problem, migraine, or seizures starting in the vision part of the brain.

name: Physical Duality
formal: Migraine aura in which the person feels they have two bodies.
simple: A rare migraine symptom where a person feels as though they have two separate bodies.

name: Pica
formal: Craving to eat non-food substances (e.g. ice — pagophagia in iron deficiency).
simple: An urge to eat things that are not food, such as ice or dirt, sometimes linked to iron deficiency.

name: Picture Sign
formal: Belief that people on television are really present in the room; dementia (DLB/Alzheimer's).
simple: Believing that people seen on television are actually present in the room; seen in some forms of dementia.

name: Picture Within a Picture Sign
formal: Seeing a small moving image within the visual field (e.g. in a hemianopic quadrant); right parieto-occipital lesion.
simple: Seeing a small extra moving image inside part of the visual field, often in an area where vision is otherwise missing; from a brain lesion affecting vision.

name: Pinhole Test
formal: Viewing through a pinhole improves acuity if the loss is refractive, not neural.
simple: Looking through a tiny pinhole improves blurry vision if the cause is a focusing (refractive) problem rather than nerve or brain damage.

name: Platysma Sign
formal: Weak platysma contraction on the side of a central hemiparesis or high cervical lesion.
simple: A neck muscle contracts weakly on one side, which can point to a brain-based (rather than purely facial-nerve) cause of facial weakness.

name: Plegia
formal: Complete paralysis.
simple: Complete paralysis of a body part.

name: Pleurothotonos
formal: Lateral trunk flexion from paraspinal spasm (tetanus); Pisa syndrome is the dystonic equivalent.
simple: The trunk bends sideways from spasm of the back muscles, seen in tetanus or a related twisting posture disorder.

name: Plexopathy
formal: Lesion of the brachial or lumbosacral plexus: multiple-nerve pattern of weakness, sensory loss and pain.
simple: Damage to a network of nerves (in the shoulder or hip area) causing weakness, numbness, and pain across the arm or leg in a pattern that doesn't match a single nerve.

name: Polyopia
formal: Seeing multiple copies of an image; occipital lesions, ocular causes.
simple: Seeing multiple copies of the same image, from a problem in the brain's vision areas or sometimes the eye itself.

name: Popeye Arms
formal: Wasted biceps/triceps with preserved deltoid and forearm muscles; facioscapulohumeral dystrophy.
simple: Wasted upper and lower arm muscles with a normal-looking shoulder muscle, giving a Popeye-like appearance; seen in a specific muscular dystrophy.

name: Poriomania
formal: Wandering during a post-ictal or ictal state.
simple: Wandering off during or after a seizure without awareness of doing so.

name: Porropsia
formal: Objects appear farther away than they are.
simple: Objects appearing farther away than they actually are.

name: Postural Reflexes
formal: Righting and protective responses to perturbation (e.g. pull test); impaired in PSP/PD.
simple: The body's automatic responses that keep balance when pushed or off-center; these are impaired in Parkinson's disease and related conditions.

name: Potomania
formal: Excess beer drinking with poor diet causing dilutional hyponatraemia (risk of central pontine myelinolysis).
simple: Drinking excessive amounts of beer with poor nutrition, which can dangerously dilute the blood's sodium level.

name: Pourfour Du Petit Syndrome
formal: "Inverse Horner": mydriasis, lid retraction, exophthalmos, hyperhidrosis from sympathetic overactivity.
simple: The opposite of Horner syndrome: an overactive sympathetic nerve causes a wide pupil, retracted eyelid, bulging eye, and sweating on one side.

name: Pouting, Pout Reflex
formal: Lip pouting/pursing on tapping the lips; frontal release sign (bilateral UMN).
simple: Tapping near the lips causes an automatic pouting or pursing movement; a primitive reflex that reappears with widespread brain disease.

name: Prayer Sign
formal: Inability to oppose the palmar surfaces of the fingers with hands in the prayer position; ulnar neuropathy, contractures, diabetic cheiroarthropathy.
simple: Trouble pressing the palms and fingers fully together as if praying; seen with certain hand nerve problems or diabetes-related joint stiffening.

name: Presbyastasis
formal: Disequilibrium of ageing: imbalance without a single cause (multisensory decline).
simple: Unsteadiness that comes with older age from a combination of small declines in vision, balance, and sensation rather than one clear cause.

name: Presbycusis
formal: Age-related high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss.
simple: Gradual hearing loss, especially for high-pitched sounds, that comes with aging.

name: Presbyopia
formal: Age-related loss of accommodation (near vision).
simple: The normal age-related loss of the eye's ability to focus on close objects.

name: Pressure Provocation Test
formal: Pressure on the palmar wrist for 60 s reproduces median paraesthesia; carpal tunnel syndrome.
simple: Pressing on the wrist for about a minute brings on tingling in the hand, supporting a diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome.

name: Prevost’s Sign
formal: Acute transient conjugate gaze deviation toward the side of a frontal lesion (away from the hemiparesis) (Vulpian's sign).
simple: Both eyes briefly look toward the side of a brain injury right after a stroke, rather than toward the weak side of the body.

name: Procerus Sign
formal: Furrowed brow from procerus contraction with astonished stare; progressive supranuclear palsy.
simple: A furrowed brow with a wide-eyed, surprised-looking stare; a facial feature seen in a Parkinson's-like condition called progressive supranuclear palsy.

name: Proptosis
formal: Forward displacement of the eye; orbital mass, thyroid eye disease, carotid-cavernous fistula.
simple: The eye bulging forward out of its socket; caused by a growth behind the eye, thyroid eye disease, or an abnormal blood vessel connection.

name: Prosopagnosia
formal: Inability to recognise familiar faces; bilateral or right occipitotemporal (fusiform) lesions.
simple: An inability to recognize familiar faces, even though other vision is normal; from damage to specific face-recognition areas of the brain.

name: Proust Phenomenon
formal: Vivid autobiographical memory triggered by an odour.
simple: A vivid, detailed memory suddenly triggered by a particular smell.

name: Proximal Limb Weakness
formal: Predominant shoulder and hip girdle weakness; myopathy, NMJ disorders, some neuropathies (CIDP) and SMA.
simple: Weakness mainly in the shoulders and hips rather than the hands and feet; typical of muscle diseases and some nerve or junction disorders.

name: Pruritus
formal: Itch; neuropathic causes include small-fibre neuropathy, MS/NMOSD (paroxysmal itch), brachioradial pruritus, notalgia paraesthetica.
simple: Itching; when caused by nerve problems it can come from small nerve fiber damage, multiple sclerosis, or skin nerve irritation.

name: Pseudoachromatopsia
formal: Apparent colour vision loss due to optic nerve disease rather than cortical achromatopsia.
simple: Apparent loss of color vision that is actually due to optic nerve disease rather than a brain-based color processing problem.

name: Pseudoathetosis
formal: Writhing finger movements when the eyes are closed due to loss of proprioception (sensory ataxia).
simple: Slow, writhing finger movements that appear when the eyes are closed, caused by loss of the body's sense of limb position rather than a true movement disorder.

name: Pseudo-Babinski Sign
formal: Dystonic great toe extension on plantar stimulation (striatal toe) — not a true corticospinal Babinski sign.
simple: An upward-turning big toe from an abnormal muscle spasm rather than the usual nerve pathway problem behind a true Babinski sign.

name: Pseudochoreoathetosis
formal: Chorea-like movements from severe proprioceptive loss.
simple: Jerky, writhing movements that mimic chorea but are actually caused by severe loss of limb-position sense rather than a movement disorder.

name: Pseudodementia
formal: Cognitive impairment due to depression (or other psychiatric illness) mimicking dementia.
simple: Memory and thinking problems that look like dementia but are actually caused by depression or another treatable mental health condition.

name: Pseudohallucination
formal: Hallucination recognised as unreal by the patient (insight preserved), or vivid imagery.
simple: A vivid hallucination-like experience where the person knows it isn't real, unlike a true hallucination.

name: Pseudomyotonia
formal: Slow relaxation not due to myotonia (e.g. neuromyotonia, hypothyroidism).
simple: Muscles that relax slowly for a reason other than true myotonia, such as an underactive thyroid or nerve hyperexcitability.

name: Pseudopapilloedema
formal: Elevated disc appearance without true swelling (drusen, tilted disc, myelinated fibres).
simple: An optic nerve that looks swollen on exam but isn't actually swollen, due to a structural variation rather than true pressure buildup.

name: Pseudoptosis
formal: Apparent ptosis from other causes (e.g. hypotropia, dermatochalasis, blepharospasm, contralateral lid retraction).
simple: A droopy-looking eyelid caused by something other than true eyelid muscle weakness, such as excess skin or spasm.

name: Pseudoradicular Syndrome
formal: Radicular-like sensory symptoms from a thalamic or cortical lesion (e.g. C8-like thalamic sensory loss).
simple: Numbness that follows a nerve-root-like pattern but is actually caused by a brain lesion rather than a pinched nerve root.

name: Pseudo-Von Graefe’s Sign
formal: Lid elevation on attempted downgaze or adduction from aberrant III nerve regeneration.
simple: The eyelid unexpectedly lifts when looking down or inward, from nerves regrowing incorrectly after a third cranial nerve injury.

name: Pulfrich Phenomenon
formal: Pendulum swinging straight appears to move in an ellipse; asymmetric optic nerve conduction (optic neuritis).
simple: A swinging object appears to move in an oval path instead of straight back and forth, because one eye sends visual signals slightly slower than the other, as in optic nerve inflammation.

name: Punding
formal: Complex, repetitive, purposeless behaviours (sorting, dismantling) with dopaminergic therapy in PD.
simple: Repetitive, purposeless behaviors like sorting or taking things apart, sometimes seen as a side effect of Parkinson's disease medications.

name: Pupil Sparing
formal: III nerve palsy without pupil involvement — typically microvascular (diabetic) rather than compressive.
simple: A third-nerve eye palsy where the pupil still reacts normally, which usually points to a small-vessel (such as diabetic) cause rather than a dangerous compressing mass.

name: Pure Word Deafness
formal: Inability to understand spoken words with preserved hearing, reading and writing; bilateral superior temporal lesions.
simple: Being unable to understand spoken words despite normal hearing and normal reading and writing ability; from damage to both sides of a hearing-related brain area.

name: Pyramidal Decussation Syndrome
formal: Weakness of one arm and the opposite leg without facial involvement (hemiplegia cruciata); lesion at the pyramidal decussation.
simple: Weakness in one arm and the opposite leg without any facial weakness; from damage right where the brain's motor pathways cross over.

name: Quadriparesis, Quadriplegia
formal: Weakness or paralysis of all four limbs; high cervical cord, brainstem, polyneuropathy, myopathy.
simple: Weakness or complete paralysis affecting all four limbs.

name: Quadrupedalism
formal: Habitual walking on all fours; congenital cerebellar hypoplasia (Uner Tan syndrome).
simple: Habitually walking on all fours instead of upright, seen in a rare condition involving underdevelopment of the cerebellum.

name: Rabbit Syndrome
formal: Rapid perioral tremor (5 Hz) like a rabbit chewing; neuroleptic-induced.
simple: A fast, fine tremor around the mouth that looks like a rabbit chewing; a side effect of certain antipsychotic medications.

name: Raccoon Eyes, Raccoon Sign
formal: Periorbital bruising; anterior cranial fossa fracture, neuroblastoma, amyloid.
simple: Bruising around both eyes, which can signal a skull fracture at the base of the skull or certain other diseases.

name: Radiculopathy
formal: Nerve root lesion: pain, dermatomal sensory loss, myotomal weakness, reflex loss.
simple: A pinched or damaged spinal nerve root causing pain, numbness in a specific strip of skin, and weakness in the muscles it controls.

name: Raynaud’s Phenomenon
formal: Episodic pallor, cyanosis then redness of digits with cold/stress; connective tissue disease, vibration, some neuropathies.
simple: Fingers or toes that turn pale, then blue, then red in response to cold or stress, from blood vessels overreacting; linked to some connective tissue and nerve conditions.

name: Recruitment
formal: Abnormal loudness growth with sound intensity; cochlear hearing loss.
simple: Sounds that seem to jump from too quiet to uncomfortably loud very quickly; a sign of inner-ear (cochlear) hearing loss.

name: Recurrent Utterances
formal: Repeated stereotyped word/syllable (e.g. "tan tan") in severe non-fluent/global aphasia.
simple: Repeating the same fixed word or sound over and over, seen in people with severe language loss after a stroke.

name: Red Ear Syndrome
formal: Attacks of burning pain and reddening of one ear; associated with migraine, upper cervical/TAC disorders.
simple: Sudden attacks of burning pain and redness in one ear, linked to migraine or certain headache disorders.

name: Retinitis Pigmentosa
formal: Retinal degeneration with bone-spicule pigment; night blindness and tunnel vision; associated neurological syndromes.
simple: An inherited eye disease where the retina slowly breaks down, causing night blindness and narrowing of side vision.

name: Retinopathy
formal: Retinal disease (diabetic, hypertensive, mitochondrial) seen on fundoscopy.
simple: Any disease of the retina, such as from diabetes or high blood pressure, seen when the eye is examined.

name: Retrocollis
formal: Backward extension of the neck; cervical dystonia, PSP.
simple: The neck pulls backward involuntarily, seen in certain neck muscle spasm disorders or PSP (a Parkinson's-like condition).

name: Reverse Sensory Geste
formal: A manoeuvre that worsens dystonia (opposite of a sensory trick).
simple: A touch or movement that makes an abnormal muscle spasm worse, the opposite of the usual trick that relieves it.

name: Revilliod’s Sign
formal: Acquired inability to wink one eye; early corticobulbar (UMN) disease.
simple: Losing the ability to wink one eye on purpose while blinking normally still works with both eyes; an early sign of a certain type of facial nerve pathway damage.

name: Riddoch’s Phenomenon
formal: Perception of moving but not stationary stimuli in a blind hemifield; occipital lesions.
simple: Being able to notice moving objects but not stationary ones in an area of otherwise blind vision; from damage to the brain's vision center.

name: Risus Sardonicus
formal: Fixed grinning from facial muscle spasm; tetanus.
simple: A fixed, grinning facial expression caused by sustained facial muscle spasm; classically seen in tetanus.

name: Rocket Sign
formal: Springs up from sitting and topples backward; postural instability in PSP.
simple: Standing up too quickly from sitting and then falling backward; a balance problem seen in a Parkinson's-like condition called PSP.

name: Roger’s Sign
formal: Numb chin syndrome: isolated mental nerve neuropathy; red flag for metastatic malignancy.
simple: Numbness limited to the chin, which can be an early warning sign of cancer that has spread to a nerve in the jaw.

name: Rolex Sign
formal: Self-winding watch stops when worn on a rigid, hypokinetic arm; early sign of parkinsonism.
simple: A self-winding watch stops running because the wearer's arm has become too stiff and moves too little; an early clue to Parkinson's disease.

name: Roos Test
formal: Elevated arm stress test: arms abducted 90°, opening and closing hands for 3 min reproduces symptoms in thoracic outlet syndrome.
simple: Holding both arms raised and repeatedly opening and closing the hands for a few minutes brings on symptoms of a nerve/blood vessel compression near the collarbone.

name: Round the Houses Sign
formal: Vertical saccades performed in an arc rather than a straight line; progressive supranuclear palsy.
simple: The eyes trace a curved path instead of moving straight up or down; seen in the Parkinson's-like condition PSP.

name: Roving Eye Movements
formal: Slow conjugate lateral wandering of the eyes; light coma with intact brainstem.
simple: Slow, drifting side-to-side eye movements seen in a lightly comatose patient whose brainstem is still working.

name: Sacral Sparing
formal: Preserved perianal sensation in a cord lesion; intramedullary lesion / incomplete injury.
simple: Feeling still present around the buttocks and genitals despite a spinal cord injury elsewhere, suggesting the injury isn't fully complete.

name: Savant Syndrome
formal: Exceptional isolated skills (memory, calculation, art) with developmental intellectual disability or autism.
simple: Having an exceptional, narrow skill such as memory or calculation alongside a developmental disability or autism.

name: Schizophasia
formal: Incoherent "word salad" speech; schizophrenia.
simple: Speech that is so disorganized it sounds like nonsense word combinations; seen in schizophrenia.

name: Schwabach Test
formal: Compares patient's and examiner's bone conduction duration; shortened in sensorineural loss.
simple: A hearing test comparing how long the patient versus the examiner can hear a tuning fork through bone; a shorter time suggests inner-ear hearing loss.

name: Scratch Test
formal: Perceiving the direction (up/down) of a scratch on the shin; tests proprioceptive/large-fibre sensation.
simple: Testing whether someone can feel and identify the direction of a light scratch on their skin, which checks a specific type of body-position sensation.

name: Seborrhoea
formal: Greasy skin; parkinsonism (autonomic).
simple: Unusually oily skin, which can be a feature of Parkinson's disease affecting the autonomic nervous system.

name: Seizures
formal: Paroxysmal abnormal neuronal discharge producing motor, sensory, autonomic or cognitive symptoms.
simple: Sudden bursts of abnormal electrical activity in the brain that can cause movement, sensory, or awareness changes.

name: Sequential Paresis
formal: "Round the clock" weakness: one arm → ipsilateral leg → contralateral leg → arm; foramen magnum / high cervical lesion.
simple: Weakness that spreads in a specific order, from one arm, to the same-side leg, to the opposite leg, to the opposite arm, seen with damage where the brainstem meets the spinal cord.

name: Setting Sun Sign
formal: Tonic downward eye deviation with upper lid retraction; dorsal midbrain compression (hydrocephalus in infants).
simple: The eyes drift downward like a sunset, with the upper eyelids pulled back showing white above the iris. Seen in babies with pressure inside the skull, often from fluid buildup (hydrocephalus).

name: Shadowing
formal: Patient follows the spouse/carer around like a shadow; dementia.
simple: A person with dementia constantly follows their spouse or caregiver from room to room like a shadow, often out of anxiety or confusion.

name: Shin-Tapping
formal: Heel tapped repeatedly on the shin before sliding down; more sensitive test for leg ataxia.
simple: The patient taps their heel on the opposite shin repeatedly before sliding it down the leg. It shows clumsiness in the leg (ataxia) better than a single slide does.

name: Sialorrhoea
formal: Drooling of saliva; PD, ALS, bulbar palsy.
simple: Excess drooling of saliva, often because swallowing is impaired. Seen in Parkinson's disease, ALS (a nerve disease that weakens muscles), and problems with the swallowing muscles.

name: Simultanagnosia
formal: Can see single items but cannot take in a whole scene at once; bilateral parieto-occipital damage (Bálint syndrome).
simple: The person can only see and understand one object at a time, even when several are in view. Caused by damage to both sides of the brain in the area that processes vision.

name: Skew Deviation
formal: Vertical ocular misalignment of supranuclear origin; brainstem/cerebellar lesion (HINTS "central" sign).
simple: One eye sits higher than the other due to a problem in the brainstem or cerebellum, not the eye muscles themselves. It is a clue to a central (brain) cause of dizziness rather than an inner-ear cause.

name: Sneezing
formal: Paroxysmal sneezing as an ictal or brainstem phenomenon; loss of sneeze in lateral medullary syndrome.
simple: Sudden bursts of sneezing can be caused by a seizure or a brainstem problem. Losing the ability to sneeze can happen with damage to the lower brainstem (lateral medullary syndrome).

name: Somatoparaphrenia
formal: Delusional belief that one's limb belongs to someone else; right parietal lesions.
simple: The person insists that their own arm or leg actually belongs to someone else. It comes from damage to the right side of the brain that handles body awareness.

name: Spasm
formal: Involuntary sustained muscle contraction (hemifacial spasm, tetany, cramps).
simple: An involuntary, sustained muscle tightening, such as one side of the face twitching, muscle cramping, or tetany (a condition causing widespread muscle spasms from low calcium).

name: Speech Apraxia
formal: Impaired planning of speech movements with inconsistent sound errors and groping; left frontal/insular lesions.
simple: Trouble planning the mouth movements needed for speech, causing inconsistent sound mistakes and visible effort or fumbling. Comes from damage to the left front part of the brain.

name: Spinal Mass Reflex
formal: Mass flexor withdrawal with autonomic discharge below a complete spinal cord transection.
simple: Below a fully injured spinal cord, a strong stimulus triggers the legs to bend up together along with sweating or other automatic reactions, even though the person cannot feel or control it.

name: Spinal Movements in Brainstem Death
formal: Reflex limb/trunk movements (e.g. Lazarus sign, triple flexion) of spinal origin compatible with brain death.
simple: Reflex movements of the arms or legs, such as one arm rising or legs briefly straightening, that can occur in someone who is brain dead. These come from the spinal cord alone and do not mean the person is recovering.

name: Spurling’s Sign
formal: Neck extension and rotation toward the symptomatic side with axial load reproduces radicular arm pain; cervical radiculopathy.
simple: Tilting and turning the neck toward the painful side while pressing down on the head brings on arm pain that shoots down in a nerve pattern. Suggests a pinched nerve in the neck.

name: Stellwag’s Sign
formal: Infrequent blinking with lid retraction; thyroid eye disease (and PSP).
simple: Blinking less often than normal along with the eyelids pulled back. Seen in thyroid eye disease and a brain condition called progressive supranuclear palsy.

name: Sternocleidomastoid Test
formal: Apparent SCM weakness ipsilateral to a functional hemiparesis (head turning toward the "weak" side).
simple: In weakness that is not due to a real nerve or brain problem, turning the head toward the "weak" side looks unusually strong, because that neck muscle is normal even though the person claims one side is weak.

name: Stiffness
formal: Subjective or objective increased resistance; rigidity, spasticity, stiff-person syndrome.
