simple: A feeling of, or actual, increased resistance when a limb is moved. Can come from rigidity (as in Parkinson's), spasticity (a nerve-related tightness), or stiff-person syndrome (a rare neuro-immune disease).

name: Stops Walking When Talking
formal: Stopping walking to answer a question (dual-task failure); predicts falls in older people and dementia.
simple: A person stops walking in order to answer a question, showing they cannot walk and talk at the same time. This predicts a higher risk of falls in older adults and in dementia.

name: Stork Legs
formal: Wasting of the lower legs with preserved thighs (inverted champagne bottle); hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy.
simple: The calves become thin while the thighs stay normal, giving legs the look of an upside-down champagne bottle. Seen in an inherited nerve disease affecting movement and sensation.

name: Stork Manoeuvre
formal: Standing on one leg with arms folded, eyes open; no wobble makes significant imbalance or pyramidal leg weakness unlikely.
simple: Standing on one leg with arms crossed and eyes open. Staying steady makes a serious balance problem or leg weakness from the brain or spine unlikely.

name: Straight Thumb Sign
formal: Inability to flex the thumb tip (FPL weakness); anterior interosseous / median nerve lesion.
simple: The person cannot bend the tip of the thumb because a specific forearm muscle is weak. Points to damage of a branch of the median nerve in the arm.

name: Striatal Hand
formal: MCP flexion, PIP extension, DIP flexion and ulnar deviation of the hand; parkinsonism.
simple: An abnormal hand posture with the knuckles bent, the middle joints straightened, the fingertip joints bent, and the hand angled toward the little-finger side. Seen in Parkinson's-type disorders.

name: String Sign
formal: Pointing to the middle of a horizontally held string; bisection error suggests a hemianopic/neglect field defect.
simple: The patient is asked to point to the middle of a string held out horizontally; pointing off-center suggests they are ignoring part of their visual field, often from a stroke affecting vision or attention.

name: Stutter, Stuttering
formal: Disrupted speech fluency with repetitions/blocks; developmental or acquired (neurogenic).
simple: Speech that is broken up by repeated sounds or blocks where words get stuck. Can start in childhood or appear later after a brain injury.

name: Sucking Reflex
formal: Sucking movement on stimulating the lips; primitive/frontal release sign.
simple: Touching the lips causes an automatic sucking motion. Normal in infants, but in adults it is a sign of frontal lobe brain dysfunction.

name: Sundowning
formal: Worsening confusion/agitation in the evening; dementia.
simple: Confusion, restlessness, or agitation that gets worse in the evening, commonly seen in people with dementia.

name: Supranuclear Gaze Palsy
formal: Limited voluntary gaze with preserved reflex (oculocephalic) movements; PSP (vertical), frontal/midbrain lesions.
simple: The person cannot move their eyes on command in certain directions, but the eyes still move normally when the head is turned. Seen in progressive supranuclear palsy and other brain lesions.

name: Suspended Sensory Loss
formal: Cape-like pain/temperature loss over shoulders/arms with normal sensation above and below; syringomyelia / central cord.
simple: Loss of pain and temperature sensation in a cape-like band across the shoulders and arms, while sensation above and below is normal. Caused by damage to the center of the spinal cord, such as a fluid-filled cyst (syringomyelia).

name: Swan Neck
formal: Thin neck from wasting of neck muscles; myotonic dystrophy.
simple: A thin, wasted-looking neck from loss of muscle bulk. Seen in myotonic dystrophy, a muscle disease.

name: Swearing
formal: Involuntary or disinhibited cursing; preserved in aphasia (automatic speech), Tourette syndrome, frontal disinhibition.
simple: Cursing that happens involuntarily or without normal self-control. Can remain intact even when other speech is lost (aphasia), or appear in Tourette syndrome or after frontal brain damage.

name: Sweat Level
formal: Level below which sweating is absent; spinal cord lesion (autonomic level).
simple: A clear line on the body below which sweating stops, marking the level of a spinal cord injury that affects the nerves controlling sweat glands.

name: Syllogomania
formal: Compulsive hoarding with domestic squalor (Diogenes syndrome); frontal dysfunction.
simple: Compulsive hoarding of objects leading to a cluttered, unsanitary home (sometimes called Diogenes syndrome). Linked to frontal lobe brain problems.

name: Synkinesia, Synkinesis
formal: Involuntary movement accompanying a voluntary one, e.g. aberrant facial regeneration after Bell's palsy.
simple: An unwanted movement that happens together with a voluntary one, such as the mouth twitching when someone tries to blink, after nerve damage heals abnormally (like after Bell's palsy).

name: Table Top Sign
formal: Cannot lay the palm and fingers flat on a tabletop; seen with ulnar claw hand, Dupuytren contracture or camptodactyly.
simple: The person cannot lay their hand completely flat on a table. Seen with a clawed hand from ulnar nerve damage, a hand condition called Dupuytren contracture, or bent finger joints (camptodactyly).

name: Tachylalia
formal: Abnormally rapid speech.
simple: Speaking abnormally fast.

name: Tachyphemia
formal: Accelerating speech with repetition (festination of speech); parkinsonism.
simple: Speech that speeds up and repeats itself more and more, similar to how walking speeds up in Parkinson's disease.

name: Tactile Agnosia
formal: Inability to recognise objects by touch despite intact primary sensation; parietal lesions.
simple: Inability to identify an object by feeling it with the eyes closed, even though basic touch sensation works fine. Comes from damage to the brain's parietal lobe.

name: Tadpole Pupils
formal: Transient segmental pupil dilatation producing a tadpole shape; benign or Horner/Adie related.
simple: A temporary bulge on one part of the pupil that makes it look like a tadpole. Usually harmless, but can relate to Horner syndrome or Adie pupil (conditions affecting pupil nerves).

name: Tasikinesia
formal: Forced walking due to inner restlessness; akathisia.
simple: An urge to keep walking because of intense inner restlessness, a feature of akathisia (often a side effect of certain medications).

name: Teichopsia
formal: Fortification spectra — zigzag scintillating visual aura of migraine.
simple: A visual disturbance of zigzag, shimmering lines, typically seen as part of a migraine aura before or during a headache.

name: Telopsia
formal: Objects appear farther away than they are.
simple: Objects look farther away than they actually are.

name: Temporal Crescent Syndrome
formal: Monocular loss of the far temporal crescent of the field; contralateral anterior calcarine cortex lesion.
simple: Loss of vision in the very outer edge of one eye's visual field. Caused by damage to the part of the brain that processes the opposite side's vision.

name: Temporal Desaturation
formal: Red targets appear desaturated in the temporal hemifields; early chiasmal compression.
simple: Red objects appear washed-out or paler when viewed to the outer sides of vision. An early sign of pressure on the optic nerve crossing point in the brain.

name: Temporal Pallor
formal: Pallor of the temporal part of the optic disc; previous optic neuritis (MS), toxic/nutritional neuropathy.
simple: The outer part of the optic nerve head looks unusually pale. Can follow a past episode of optic nerve inflammation (as in multiple sclerosis) or nerve damage from toxins or poor nutrition.

name: Terson Syndrome
formal: Vitreous/preretinal hemorrhage associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage.
simple: Bleeding inside the eye that occurs together with bleeding around the brain (subarachnoid hemorrhage).

name: Thumb Reflex
formal: Flexion of the thumb tip on tapping the flexor pollicis longus tendon (C6–C8); distal stretch reflex.
simple: Tapping a tendon in the forearm causes the thumb tip to bend, a normal reflex that tests nerves from the lower neck area.

name: Thumb Rolling Test
formal: Twiddling the thumbs: the thumb on the UMN-weak side stays relatively still; subtle corticospinal lesion.
simple: When asked to twiddle their thumbs, the thumb on the side with mild nerve-pathway weakness moves less than the other, revealing a subtle weakness from the brain or spinal cord.

name: Tic Convulsif
formal: Trigeminal neuralgia combined with hemifacial spasm, usually from vascular compression.
simple: A combination of facial nerve pain (trigeminal neuralgia) and one-sided facial muscle spasm, usually caused by a blood vessel pressing on the nerves.

name: Tilted Disc
formal: Oval, obliquely inserted optic disc with superotemporal field defects not respecting the vertical meridian; benign anomaly.
simple: The optic nerve head is oval-shaped and inserted at an angle rather than straight, causing a vision defect that doesn't follow the usual pattern. Usually a harmless anatomical variation.

name: Tinel’s Sign (Hoffmann-Tinel Sign)
formal: Tapping over a nerve reproduces tingling in its distribution; entrapment or regenerating nerve.
simple: Tapping over a nerve causes tingling that spreads along where that nerve travels. Suggests the nerve is pinched or is in the process of healing.
th: เคาะบริเวณเส้นประสาทแล้วรู้สึกเสียวแปลบไปตามแนวประสาท — บ่งชี้เส้นประสาทระคายเคือง/กำลังงอกใหม่
exam: Tap along the course of the nerve (e.g. over the carpal tunnel or cubital tunnel).
pos: Tingling in the nerve's sensory territory = focal nerve irritation or regeneration site (CTS, ulnar neuropathy).
aN: hoffmann tinel sign | tinel sign | tinel | tinel test | hoffmann tinel

det.mechanism: Demyelinated or regenerating axon sprouts are mechanically sensitive. Tapping over such a segment generates ectopic impulses that the patient feels as tingling projected into the cutaneous territory of the nerve. During regeneration, the point of maximal Tinel moves distally as axons grow.
det.technique: Using a finger or reflex hammer, tap lightly along the course of the nerve from distal to proximal, such as over the carpal tunnel, cubital tunnel or fibular head. Ask the patient to report tingling and where it is felt. Tap firmly enough to stimulate but not to cause pain.
det.interpretation: A positive sign suggests focal nerve irritability or regeneration at that site, but specificity is limited and healthy people sometimes report tingling. For carpal tunnel syndrome, accuracy is moderate. Serial testing after nerve injury, with an advancing Tinel, indicates regrowth; a static Tinel suggests neuroma formation.
pearls: An advancing Tinel after nerve repair is a sign of regeneration.
Tingling must radiate into the nerve's territory, not just local discomfort.
det.thd: Tinel sign คือเคาะตามแนวเส้นประสาทแล้วรู้สึกเสียวแปลบลงไปตามบริเวณที่เส้นประสาทนั้นเลี้ยง เกิดเพราะใยประสาทที่ถูกกดหรือกำลังงอกใหม่ไวต่อแรงกด ใช้ช่วยหาตำแหน่งรอยโรค เช่น CTS หรือ ulnar neuropathy แต่ความจำเพาะไม่สูง หลังเส้นประสาทบาดเจ็บถ้าจุด Tinel เลื่อนลงไปเรื่อย ๆ แสดงว่าเส้นประสาทกำลังงอก

name: Todd’s Paralysis, Todd’s Paresis
formal: Transient focal weakness after a seizure, resolving within hours.
simple: Temporary weakness of part of the body after a seizure, which goes away on its own within a few hours.

name: Toe Walking
formal: Walking on the toes; Duchenne dystrophy, spasticity, idiopathic.
simple: Walking on the toes rather than the whole foot. Can be seen in muscular dystrophy, muscle tightness from nerve disease (spasticity), or simply as a habit with no underlying disease.

name: Tongue Biting
formal: Lateral tongue bite favours generalised tonic-clonic seizure; tip biting may occur in non-epileptic attacks.
simple: Biting the side of the tongue suggests a full-body convulsive seizure, while biting just the tip is more typical of episodes that look like seizures but aren't (non-epileptic attacks).

name: Tonic Spasms
formal: Brief painful stereotyped tonic posturing of a limb, often triggered by movement; multiple sclerosis/NMOSD.
simple: Brief, painful episodes where a limb tightens into an abnormal position, often triggered by movement. Seen in multiple sclerosis and related nerve conditions.

name: Topographagnosia
formal: Getting lost in familiar surroundings (landmark or route agnosia); right medial occipitotemporal/parahippocampal lesions.
simple: Getting lost even in familiar places because landmarks or routes are no longer recognized. Caused by damage to a specific area on the right side of the brain.

name: Transcortical Aphasias
formal: Aphasias with preserved repetition (motor, sensory, mixed); watershed lesions.
simple: Types of language problems where the person can still repeat words said to them, even though other aspects of speech are impaired. Usually from strokes affecting blood-flow border zones of the brain.

name: Triplopia
formal: Seeing three images; unusual ocular motor palsies or monocular causes.
simple: Seeing three copies of a single object, an unusual problem with eye movement or with one eye alone.

name: Trismus
formal: Inability to open the mouth from masseter spasm; tetanus, dystonia, local causes.
simple: Inability to open the mouth because the jaw-clenching muscle is in spasm. Causes include tetanus, dystonia (abnormal muscle contractions), or a local mouth/jaw problem.

name: Trombone Tongue
formal: Tongue repeatedly protrudes and retracts involuntarily (motor impersistence); Huntington's chorea.
simple: The tongue repeatedly darts in and out involuntarily and cannot be held still. A feature of Huntington's disease.

name: Trömner’s Sign
formal: Flicking the pad of the middle finger causes thumb and finger flexion; UMN sign like Hoffmann.
simple: Flicking the middle fingertip downward causes the thumb and fingers to twitch and bend. Like Hoffmann's sign, it suggests a problem in the brain or spinal cord pathways controlling movement.

name: Trousseau’s Sign
formal: Carpal spasm induced by inflating a BP cuff above systolic for 3 min; hypocalcemia (latent tetany).
simple: Inflating a blood pressure cuff on the arm for a few minutes causes the hand to cramp into a claw shape, revealing low blood calcium.

name: Troxler Effect
formal: A fixated peripheral stimulus fades from perception — normal sensory adaptation.
simple: If you stare at one spot, an object off to the side that doesn't move will seem to disappear. This is a normal quirk of how vision works, not a disease.

name: Tullio Phenomenon
formal: Vertigo or nystagmus induced by loud sounds; superior canal dehiscence, perilymph fistula.
simple: Loud sounds trigger dizziness or abnormal eye movements. Caused by an abnormal opening in the inner ear's balance canal or a related leak.

name: Uhthoff’s Phenomenon
formal: Transient worsening of symptoms (e.g. vision) with heat or exercise; demyelination (MS).
simple: Symptoms like blurred vision temporarily get worse with heat or exercise, then improve once cooled down. A hallmark of multiple sclerosis.

name: Unterberger’s Sign
formal: Stepping on the spot with eyes closed causes rotation toward the side of a peripheral vestibular lesion (Fukuda test).
simple: Marching in place with eyes closed causes the person to slowly turn toward the side of a damaged inner-ear balance organ.

name: Upper Motor Neurone (UMN) Syndrome
formal: Weakness with spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantars, clonus, pyramidal-pattern weakness.
simple: A pattern of weakness caused by damage to the brain or spinal cord's movement pathways, marked by stiffness, overactive reflexes, an abnormal toe reflex, and jerking (clonus).

name: Urinary Retention
formal: Inability to empty the bladder; cauda equina/conus, spinal cord, autonomic neuropathy, MSA.
simple: Difficulty or inability to empty the bladder. Can result from nerve damage in the lower spine, spinal cord disease, or conditions affecting the nerves controlling bladder function.

name: Useless Hand of Oppenheim
formal: Clumsy "useless" hand from loss of proprioception due to a cervical dorsal column plaque; MS.
simple: A hand that becomes clumsy and "useless" because the person has lost the sense of where their fingers are in space, from damage to a specific nerve pathway in the neck (often from multiple sclerosis).

name: Utilization Behaviour
formal: Compulsive use of objects placed within reach without instruction; frontal lobe lesions.
simple: Automatically picking up and using an object just because it is within reach, even without being told to. Seen with damage to the front part of the brain.

name: Valsalva Manoeuvre
formal: Forced expiration against a closed glottis; tests cardiovagal/adrenergic autonomic function.
simple: Straining as if holding your breath and bearing down. Used to test how well the heart rate and blood vessels are controlled by the autonomic nervous system.

name: Vertigo
formal: Illusion of movement (spinning) of self or surroundings; peripheral or central vestibular dysfunction.
simple: A false sensation that you or your surroundings are spinning or moving. Comes from a problem in the inner ear or in the brain's balance centers.

name: Vestibulo-Ocular Reflexes
formal: Eye movements compensating for head movement; tested by head impulse, doll's eyes, calorics.
simple: Automatic eye movements that keep vision steady when the head moves. Tested by quickly turning the head, moving the eyes with the head turned (doll's eyes), or squirting water in the ear (calorics).

name: Visual Agnosia
formal: Inability to recognise objects visually despite adequate vision (apperceptive or associative).
simple: Inability to recognize objects by sight even though the eyes themselves see normally. The problem lies in how the brain interprets what is seen.

name: Visual Disorientation
formal: Inability to localise objects in space visually; bilateral parietal lesions.
simple: Trouble figuring out where objects are located in space just by looking at them. Caused by damage to both sides of the brain's parietal lobes.

name: Visual Extinction
formal: Failure to see a stimulus in one hemifield only on simultaneous bilateral stimulation; parietal lesions.
simple: A stimulus is seen fine on its own, but disappears from awareness when something is shown at the same time on the other side. A subtle sign of brain damage affecting attention.

name: Visual Form Agnosia
formal: Inability to perceive shape despite preserved acuity and colour; e.g. carbon monoxide poisoning.
simple: Trouble recognizing the shape of objects even though eyesight and color vision are otherwise fine, as can happen after carbon monoxide poisoning.

name: Visual Snow
formal: Persistent tiny flickering dots throughout the visual field ("TV static"), often with palinopsia, photophobia, migraine.
simple: A constant field of flickering dots covering all of vision, like TV static. Often comes with afterimages, light sensitivity, and migraines.

name: Von Graefe’s Sign
formal: Lid lag on downgaze; thyroid eye disease.
simple: When looking down, the upper eyelid doesn't drop as quickly as the eye does, leaving a gap. A feature of thyroid-related eye disease.

name: Warm-Up Phenomenon
formal: Myotonia decreases with repeated contraction; myotonia congenita.
simple: Muscle stiffness (myotonia) improves the more the muscle is used. A feature of the muscle disease myotonia congenita.

name: Wartenberg’s Pendulum Test
formal: Legs dangling from the couch are released and the pendular swings observed: reduced/irregular swings in rigidity or spasticity.
simple: The examiner releases the lower legs from a raised position and watches how they swing; reduced or irregular swinging suggests muscle stiffness from rigidity or spasticity.

name: Wartenberg’s Sign (1)
formal: Little finger held abducted from weak third palmar interosseous; ulnar neuropathy.
simple: The little finger sticks out away from the others because a specific hand muscle is weak, a sign of ulnar nerve damage.

name: Weakness
formal: Reduced muscle power; pattern localises UMN, LMN, NMJ or muscle.
simple: Reduced strength in a muscle. Where and how it appears helps doctors figure out if the problem is in the brain, spinal nerves, the connection between nerve and muscle, or the muscle itself.

name: Wheelchair Sign
formal: Early need for a wheelchair in parkinsonism (falls); suggests atypical parkinsonism (PSP, MSA) rather than PD.
simple: Needing a wheelchair early on in a Parkinson's-like illness, usually from frequent falls. Suggests a more aggressive Parkinson's-like disorder rather than classic Parkinson's disease.

name: Wilbrand’s Sign
formal: Tracing letters with a finger to help reading; pure alexia.
simple: Tracing letters in the air or on a surface with a finger to help make sense of written words, seen in a condition where a person can't read despite normal vision (pure alexia).

name: Wing-Beating Tremor
formal: Coarse proximal tremor of abducted arms like flapping wings; Wilson disease.
simple: A large, slow shaking of the arms when held out and lifted, resembling flapping wings. Seen in Wilson disease, a genetic copper-buildup disorder.

name: Witzelsucht
formal: Inappropriate facetious humour and punning; frontal (orbitofrontal) lesions.
simple: Making inappropriate jokes or puns at odd times, without understanding it's out of place. Comes from damage to the front part of the brain.

name: Woltman’s Sign
formal: Slow-relaxing ("hung-up") tendon reflexes; hypothyroidism.
simple: Tendon reflexes (like the ankle jerk) that are slow to relax after being triggered. A classic sign of an underactive thyroid gland.

name: Writer’s Cramp
formal: Task-specific focal hand dystonia during writing.
simple: Abnormal, involuntary muscle contractions in the hand that happen only during writing, a type of task-specific dystonia.

name: Xanthopsia
formal: Objects appear yellow; digoxin toxicity.
simple: Objects appear tinted yellow, a known side effect of digoxin (a heart medication) toxicity.

name: Xerophthalmia, Xerostomia
formal: Dry eyes and mouth; Sjögren syndrome, autonomic neuropathy, anticholinergics.
simple: Dryness of the eyes and mouth. Can be caused by Sjögren syndrome (an autoimmune condition), nerve problems affecting glands, or certain medications.

name: Yawning
formal: Excessive yawning; brainstem lesions, seizures, drugs, before vasovagal syncope.
simple: Yawning much more often than usual. Can be linked to brainstem problems, seizures, certain drugs, or as a warning sign before fainting.

name: Yips
formal: Task-specific dystonia in golfers during putting/chipping.
simple: A task-specific loss of fine motor control, such as golfers suddenly being unable to putt smoothly, thought to be a form of focal dystonia.

name: Yo- Yo-Ing
formal: Sudden unpredictable swings between "off" immobility and dyskinesia in long-term levodopa-treated PD.
simple: Unpredictable swings between being unable to move ("off") and having excess involuntary movements ("on") in people who have taken levodopa for Parkinson's disease for a long time.

name: Zooagnosia
formal: Inability to recognise familiar animals; visual agnosia variant.
simple: Trouble recognizing familiar animals by sight, a specific form of visual agnosia (general object-recognition difficulty).

name: Zoom Effect
formal: Migraine aura with images repeatedly enlarging and shrinking.
simple: A visual migraine aura in which images seem to repeatedly grow larger and then shrink.

name: Amblyopia
formal: Reduced visual acuity from abnormal visual development in childhood ("lazy eye"), not correctable by lenses.
simple: Reduced vision in an eye from abnormal visual development in childhood ("lazy eye"), which glasses alone cannot fully fix.

name: Arm Drop
formal: Face–hand test: the "paralysed" hand dropped over the face avoids hitting it in functional weakness/unresponsiveness.
simple: A test where the "paralyzed" hand is dropped over the person's face; if it swerves to avoid hitting the face, the weakness is likely not from a real nerve or brain problem.

name: Automatic Writing Behavior
formal: Compulsive writing in response to visual/tactile stimuli; frontal lesions.
simple: Compulsively writing whenever something is seen or felt, without meaning to. Comes from damage to the front part of the brain.

name: Beevor’s Sign
formal: Upward movement of the umbilicus on flexing the neck/sitting up from lying, due to weak lower abdominal muscles (lesion ~T10); also FSHD.
simple: When lying down and lifting the head or trying to sit up, the belly button moves upward because the lower abdominal muscles are weak. Suggests a mid-back spinal cord problem, or can occur in a form of muscular dystrophy.
th: ยกศีรษะจากท่านอนแล้วสะดือเลื่อนขึ้น — กล้ามเนื้อท้องส่วนล่างอ่อนแรงกว่าส่วนบน
exam: Patient supine raises the head against resistance or attempts a sit-up; watch the umbilicus.
pos: Upward umbilical movement = weak lower rectus abdominis (T10–T12 lesion or myopathy, classically FSHD).

det.mechanism: The umbilicus sits at the T10 dermatomal and myotomal level. If the lower rectus abdominis (below T10) is weaker than the upper portion, contraction of the stronger upper fibres pulls the umbilicus upward during trunk flexion.
det.technique: With the patient supine, ask them to lift the head toward the chest or attempt a partial sit-up, ideally against light resistance on the forehead. Watch the umbilicus closely; upward excursion of more than about 1 cm is positive. Obesity and abdominal scars make it hard to judge.
det.interpretation: A positive sign suggests a spinal cord or root lesion around T10–T11, or a myopathy preferentially affecting lower abdominal muscles. In neuromuscular clinics it is highly suggestive of FSHD, where it may be present before limb weakness, though it also occurs in some LGMDs, Pompe disease and inclusion body myositis. Downward movement suggests upper abdominal weakness.
pearls: Beevor sign in an ambulant patient with facial or scapular weakness: think FSHD.
Also look for a T10 sensory level in suspected cord lesions.
det.thd: Beevor sign คือเมื่อผู้ป่วยนอนหงายยกศีรษะแล้วสะดือเลื่อนขึ้น เพราะกล้ามเนื้อท้องส่วนล่าง (ใต้ T10) อ่อนกว่าส่วนบน บ่งชี้รอยโรคไขสันหลังหรือรากประสาทระดับ T10 หรือโรคกล้ามเนื้อ โดยเฉพาะ FSHD ซึ่งอาจพบก่อนแขนขาอ่อนแรง

name: Carphologia
formal: Aimless plucking at bedclothes; delirium.
simple: Aimlessly picking or plucking at bedsheets or clothing, often seen in people who are severely confused (delirium).

name: Cataplexy
formal: Sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion (laughter) with preserved consciousness; narcolepsy type 1.
simple: Sudden loss of muscle strength triggered by strong emotion like laughing, while the person stays fully awake and aware. A feature of narcolepsy.

name: Catathrenia
formal: Groaning during expiration in sleep.
simple: Making groaning sounds while breathing out during sleep.

name: Cauda Equina Syndrome
formal: Saddle anesthesia, sphincter dysfunction and asymmetric LMN leg weakness with reflex loss.
simple: Numbness in the area that would touch a saddle, loss of bladder or bowel control, and uneven leg weakness with reduced reflexes, from compression of nerves at the bottom of the spinal canal.

name: Cerebellopontine Angle Syndrome
formal: Ipsilateral V, VII, VIII nerve involvement ± cerebellar signs; vestibular schwannoma, meningioma.
simple: Problems with the nerves for facial sensation, facial movement, and hearing/balance on one side, sometimes with clumsiness, from a growth such as a tumor on the hearing nerve.

name: Cherry Red Spot at the Macula
formal: Red fovea surrounded by pale retina: central retinal artery occlusion or lipid storage diseases (Tay-Sachs).
simple: A bright red spot at the center of the retina surrounded by pale tissue, seen with a blocked blood vessel in the eye or certain inherited fat-storage diseases.
nN: cherry red spot at the macula

name: Chicken Wings
formal: Bilateral scapular winging with arms abducted; facioscapulohumeral dystrophy.
simple: Both shoulder blades stick out prominently when the arms are lifted out to the sides. A sign of a muscular dystrophy affecting the face, shoulders, and upper arms.

name: Circumlocution
formal: Talking around a word that cannot be retrieved (describing it instead); anomia.
simple: Talking around a word a person can't quite recall, describing it instead of naming it. A sign of word-finding difficulty (anomia).

name: Corneopterygoid Reflex
formal: Same as corneomandibular reflex — jaw movement on corneal stimulation.
simple: The jaw moves when the surface of the eye is touched, the same reflex known as the corneomandibular reflex.

name: Coup de Sabre
formal: Linear scleroderma of the forehead/scalp ("sabre cut"); associated with hemifacial atrophy and seizures.
simple: A line-shaped scar-like patch on the forehead or scalp, as if from a sword cut, from a form of localized skin thickening (scleroderma) that can be linked with facial shrinkage on one side and seizures.

name: Crossed straight leg raise
formal: Raising the unaffected leg reproduces pain in the affected leg; large disc herniation.
simple: Lifting the pain-free leg brings on pain in the other, already-painful leg. Suggests a large disc herniation pressing on a nerve.

name: Czarnecki’s Sign
formal: Pupil constriction on attempted eye movement from aberrant III nerve regeneration.
simple: The pupil narrows when the eye tries to move, due to nerve fibers regrowing abnormally after damage to the nerve controlling eye movement (the third cranial nerve).

name: Delusion
formal: Fixed false belief held despite contrary evidence and not culturally explained.
simple: A firmly held false belief that persists despite clear evidence against it and isn't explained by the person's culture or beliefs.

name: Diaphoresis
formal: Excessive sweating.
simple: Sweating more than normal.

name: Dorsal Guttering
formal: Wasting of dorsal interossei producing grooves on the back of the hand; ulnar / C8–T1 lesions.
simple: Visible grooves on the back of the hand from wasting of the small muscles between the fingers. Comes from damage to the ulnar nerve or the lower neck nerve roots.

name: Dropped Head Syndrome
formal: Severe neck extensor weakness with chin on chest; MG, ALS, myositis, isolated neck extensor myopathy.
simple: The neck muscles that hold the head up become severely weak, so the chin drops toward the chest. Seen in myasthenia gravis, ALS, muscle inflammation, or a muscle disease limited to the neck.

name: Dystrophic pattern of weakness
formal: Proximal, symmetric weakness with preserved reflexes early in the course; muscular dystrophy.
simple: Weakness that is symmetric and affects the muscles closer to the body (shoulders, hips) first, while reflexes stay fairly normal early on. Typical of muscular dystrophy.

name: Eyelid Apraxia
formal: Difficulty opening the eyes voluntarily despite no weakness; PSP, PD, frontal lesions (levator inhibition).
simple: Trouble opening the eyes on purpose even though the eyelid muscles aren't actually weak. Seen in progressive supranuclear palsy, Parkinson's disease, or frontal brain lesions.

name: Fast Micrographia
formal: Small handwriting without progressive decrement; not typical of PD.
simple: Small handwriting that stays small and doesn't get progressively smaller as writing continues; this pattern is not typical of Parkinson's disease.

name: Forced Upgaze
formal: Tonic upward deviation of the eyes; oculogyric crisis, hypoxic coma.
simple: The eyes are pulled upward and stuck there involuntarily. Seen in oculogyric crisis (a drug reaction) or after severe lack of oxygen to the brain.

name: Gaze Palsy
formal: Inability to move both eyes together in one direction; supranuclear, nuclear or internuclear lesions.
simple: Both eyes cannot move together in a certain direction. Can come from a problem in the eye-movement control centers of the brainstem or the connections between them.

name: Gegenhalten
formal: Paratonia: variable resistance to passive movement that increases with the speed/force of movement; frontal lobe dysfunction, dementia.
simple: Resistance to having a limb moved passively that isn't steady, but instead increases the harder or faster you try to move it. A sign of frontal lobe brain dysfunction, including some dementias.

name: Glossolalia
formal: Speech-like utterances without meaning ("speaking in tongues").
simple: Speech-like sounds and syllables that have no real meaning, sometimes described as "speaking in tongues."

name: Hemialexia
formal: Alexia confined to one visual hemifield; callosal lesions.
simple: Difficulty reading words only on one side of a page or one half of the field of vision. Caused by damage to the fibers connecting the two halves of the brain.

name: Hemifacial Atrophy
formal: Progressive wasting of one side of the face (Parry–Romberg syndrome).
simple: Gradual wasting away of tissue on one side of the face over time (Parry-Romberg syndrome).

name: Hemifacial Spasm
formal: Unilateral irregular clonic/tonic contractions of facial muscles; vascular compression of the facial nerve.
simple: Involuntary, irregular twitching of one half of the face, usually caused by a blood vessel compressing the facial nerve.

name: Heterochromia Iridis
formal: Irises of different colours; congenital Horner syndrome, Waardenburg syndrome.
simple: The two eyes (or parts of one eye) are different colors. Can be present from birth, associated with a form of Horner syndrome, or with Waardenburg syndrome (a genetic condition).

name: Hyperekplexia
formal: Exaggerated startle response; glycine receptor mutations or brainstem lesions.
simple: An excessive, exaggerated flinch or startle response to sudden noise or touch, from a genetic condition affecting nerve signaling or from a brainstem problem.

name: Hypersomnolence
formal: Excessive daytime sleepiness; narcolepsy, sleep apnea, hypothalamic lesions.
simple: Feeling excessively sleepy during the day. Seen in narcolepsy, sleep apnea, or damage to a sleep-regulating part of the brain.

name: Hyposexuality
formal: Reduced sexual drive.
simple: A reduced interest in sex.

name: Imitation Behavior
formal: Spontaneous imitation of the examiner's gestures without instruction; frontal lesions.
simple: Copying the examiner's gestures automatically, without being asked to. Comes from damage to the front part of the brain.

name: Impersistence
formal: Inability to sustain a posture or action (e.g. eye closure, tongue protrusion); right hemisphere, chorea (motor impersistence).
simple: Inability to hold a position or keep doing an action, like keeping the eyes shut or the tongue stuck out. Seen with right-brain damage or in conditions with jerky, involuntary movements like chorea.

name: Incontinence
formal: Loss of bladder/bowel control; frontal lesions, spinal cord, cauda equina.
simple: Losing control over the bladder or bowels. Can come from frontal brain damage, spinal cord problems, or nerve compression at the base of the spine.

name: Jargon Aphasia
formal: Fluent speech full of paraphasias and neologisms, often with poor insight; Wernicke-type aphasia.
simple: Speech that flows easily but is full of wrong or made-up words, often with the person not realizing anything is wrong. Typical of a type of language disorder from damage to a brain area involved in understanding speech.

name: Lateral Medullary Syndrome
formal: Wallenberg: ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, Horner, ataxia, bulbar palsy + contralateral body pain/temperature loss; PICA/vertebral occlusion.
simple: A stroke pattern causing loss of pain and temperature sensation on one side of the face and the opposite side of the body, plus a droopy eyelid with a small pupil, unsteady movement, and swallowing/voice problems, from blockage of a small artery near the brainstem.

name: Lazarus Sign
formal: Spinal reflex movement of the arms (raising, crossing) in brain death; does not exclude the diagnosis.
simple: Arm movements, such as rising up or crossing over the chest, that occur reflexively from the spinal cord in a person who has been declared brain dead. This does not mean the person is recovering.

name: Lid Lag
formal: Upper lid lags behind the globe on downgaze; thyroid eye disease, also PSP.
simple: The upper eyelid is slow to follow the eye when looking downward. Seen in thyroid eye disease and also in progressive supranuclear palsy.

name: Macrographia
formal: Abnormally large handwriting; cerebellar disease.
simple: Handwriting that is abnormally large, seen in some cerebellar (balance-control brain area) diseases.

name: Masticatory Claudication
formal: Jaw pain on chewing relieved by rest; giant cell arteritis.
simple: Jaw pain that comes on with chewing and goes away with rest, similar to leg cramping from poor blood flow. A warning sign of giant cell arteritis, an inflammation of blood vessels.

name: Mirror Movements
formal: Involuntary movements of the opposite limb mirroring voluntary movement; Klippel-Feil, Kallmann, PD, stroke.
simple: Involuntary movements on one side of the body that copy an intentional movement made on the other side. Seen in certain genetic conditions, Parkinson's disease, or after a stroke.

name: Mitgehen
formal: Limb follows the lightest pressure from the examiner despite instruction to resist (facilitatory paratonia); frontal dysfunction.
simple: A limb keeps moving in whatever direction the examiner pushes it, even very lightly, even though the patient was told to resist. A sign of frontal brain dysfunction.

name: Muscle Hypertrophy
formal: Enlarged muscles: true (myotonia congenita, neuromyotonia) or pseudohypertrophy (dystrophies).
simple: Muscles that look larger than normal, either from a real increase in muscle tissue (as in some muscle-stiffness disorders) or from fat and connective tissue replacing muscle in some muscular dystrophies.

name: Myerson sign
formal: Non-habituating blink to repetitive glabellar tap; parkinsonism.
simple: Tapping repeatedly between the eyebrows keeps triggering a blink instead of the blink response fading out, as it normally would. Seen in Parkinsonism.

name: Myorhythmia
formal: Slow (1–4 Hz) rhythmic repetitive movement of limbs/face; oculomasticatory myorhythmia = Whipple disease.
simple: A slow, rhythmic, repetitive movement of a limb or the face. When it involves the eyes and chewing muscles together, it points strongly to Whipple disease, a rare infection.

name: Nyctalopia
formal: Night blindness; retinitis pigmentosa, vitamin A deficiency.
simple: Difficulty seeing in low light or at night. Seen in retinitis pigmentosa (an inherited eye disease) or vitamin A deficiency.

name: Obscurations
formal: Seconds-long greying out of vision with posture change; papilledema (raised ICP).
simple: Brief episodes, lasting seconds, where vision greys out or dims, often triggered by standing up or bending over. A sign of raised pressure inside the skull, as with swelling of the optic nerve (papilledema).

name: Ocular Tilt Reaction
formal: Head tilt, skew deviation and ocular torsion toward the lower eye; utricle / vestibular pathway lesion.
simple: The head tilts to one side, one eye sits lower than the other, and the eyes rotate slightly, all toward the side of a lower eye. Comes from a problem in the inner ear's balance organs or their brain pathways.

name: One-and-a-Half Syndrome
formal: Ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy plus INO — only abduction of the contralateral eye remains; dorsal pontine lesion.
simple: One eye cannot look left or right at all, and the other eye can only look outward (not inward), from a brainstem lesion affecting the eye-movement pathways.

name: Optic Ataxia
formal: Misreaching for visual targets despite normal strength and sensation; superior parietal lesions (Balint).
simple: Reaching for an object with the hand consistently misses its target under visual guidance, even though strength and basic sensation are normal. Comes from damage to the upper parietal lobe.

name: Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN), Optokinetic Response
formal: Nystagmus induced by a moving striped drum/tape; tests pursuit/saccades, asymmetry in parietal lesions, preserved in functional blindness.
simple: Rhythmic eye movements produced by watching a repeating pattern move past, like looking out a train window. Used to test how well the eyes track and jump between targets, and can reveal brain damage or confirm that someone claiming blindness can actually see.

name: Palatal Myoclonus
formal: Palatal tremor: rhythmic palatal movement ± ear click; Guillain–Mollaret triangle lesion (symptomatic) or essential.
simple: Rhythmic, repetitive movement of the soft palate at the back of the mouth, sometimes with a clicking sound in the ear. Can be caused by damage to a specific brainstem-cerebellum circuit, or occur with no clear cause.

name: Paramyotonia
formal: Myotonia that worsens with repeated exercise and cold; paramyotonia congenita (SCN4A).
simple: Muscle stiffness that gets worse, rather than better, the more the muscle is used, and also worsens in the cold. Seen in a genetic muscle condition called paramyotonia congenita.

name: Phalen’s Sign
formal: Wrist flexion for about 60 s reproduces median-territory paresthesia; carpal tunnel syndrome.
simple: Holding the wrist bent for about a minute brings on tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers. A sign of carpal tunnel syndrome, where a wrist nerve is compressed.
th: งอข้อมือค้าง 1 นาที แล้วชานิ้วโป้งถึงนิ้วนาง — สนับสนุน carpal tunnel syndrome
exam: Hold both wrists fully flexed (backs of hands together) for 60 seconds.
pos: Paraesthesia in the median distribution supports carpal tunnel syndrome; confirm with nerve conduction.
aN: phalen | phalen test | wrist flexion test

det.mechanism: Full wrist flexion raises pressure in the carpal tunnel and narrows its cross-sectional area, further compressing an already vulnerable median nerve. Ischaemia of the compressed segment provokes ectopic sensory discharges perceived as tingling in median-supplied digits.
det.technique: Ask the patient to press the backs of both hands together with wrists fully flexed and elbows relaxed, holding for 60 seconds. Note the time to onset and distribution of paraesthesia. Avoid forcing the wrist in patients with arthritis; the reverse Phalen (prayer position) is an alternative.
det.interpretation: Tingling in the thumb, index, middle and radial ring finger supports carpal tunnel syndrome, but sensitivity and specificity are only moderate (roughly 50–80% across studies). Tingling in the little finger points elsewhere. Clinical findings should be confirmed with nerve conduction studies before surgery, which also grade severity.
pearls: Ask exactly which fingers tingle — little finger involvement argues against CTS.
Combine with thenar strength and sensory testing.
det.thd: Phalen sign คือการงอข้อมือเต็มที่ค้าง 60 วินาที ทำให้ความดันใน carpal tunnel สูงขึ้นและกดเส้นประสาท median จนชาบริเวณนิ้วโป้งถึงครึ่งนิ้วนาง ผลบวกสนับสนุน carpal tunnel syndrome แต่ความไวและความจำเพาะปานกลาง ควรยืนยันด้วยการตรวจ NCS โดยเฉพาะก่อนผ่าตัด

name: Phonophobia
formal: Sensitivity/discomfort to sound; migraine, meningitis.
simple: Discomfort or pain triggered by ordinary sounds. Seen in migraine and in meningitis (infection around the brain).

name: Phosphene
formal: Flash of light seen without light stimulus (e.g. on eye movement in optic neuritis).
simple: Seeing a flash or flicker of light without any actual light being present, sometimes triggered by eye movement in inflammation of the optic nerve.

name: Pinch Sign
formal: Inability to make an "O" with thumb and index tips (pinch with pads flat); anterior interosseous nerve palsy.
simple: Instead of forming a rounded "O" shape by pinching the thumb and index finger together, the person can only press the flat pads together, because a hand nerve controlling fingertip movement is not working. A sign of damage to a branch of a forearm nerve.

name: Priapism
formal: Persistent painful erection; acute spinal cord injury, sickle cell disease.
simple: A painful erection that will not go away on its own. Can be caused by a spinal cord injury or by sickle cell disease.

name: Pseudo-Argyll Robertson Pupil
formal: Light–near dissociation from causes other than syphilis (e.g. aberrant III regeneration, diabetes, Adie).
simple: The pupils react normally to near objects but poorly to light, similar to a pattern classically linked to syphilis, but here caused by something else, such as abnormal nerve regrowth, diabetes, or Adie pupil.

name: Pseudo-Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia
formal: INO-like adduction weakness from non-MLF causes, typically myasthenia gravis.
simple: A pattern that looks like a specific eye-movement brainstem problem (one eye failing to turn inward), but is actually caused by myasthenia gravis, a disease affecting the nerve-muscle connection, not the brainstem itself.

name: Pseudo-One-and-a-Half Syndrome
formal: One-and-a-half pattern from myasthenia or other non-pontine causes.
simple: A pattern of eye movement problems that mimics the "one-and-a-half syndrome" brainstem pattern but is actually caused by myasthenia gravis or another non-brainstem condition.
nN: pseudo one and a half syndrome

name: Pull test (retropulsion)
formal: More than two backward steps or a fall after a sudden shoulder pull; postural instability in parkinsonism.
simple: The examiner gives a sudden pull backward on the shoulders; taking more than two steps back or falling shows poor balance, common in Parkinson's-type disorders.

name: Reduplicative Paramnesia
formal: Belief that a place (e.g. the hospital) exists in duplicate; right hemisphere + frontal lesions.
simple: A false belief that a familiar place, like the hospital someone is in, actually exists in two identical copies somewhere else. Comes from damage to the right side and front of the brain.

name: Retinal Venous Pulsation
formal: Spontaneous venous pulsation at the disc; its presence suggests normal ICP.
simple: A normal, gentle pulsing seen in the veins at the back of the eye. Its presence is reassuring evidence that pressure inside the skull is not elevated.

name: Right-Left Disorientation
formal: Inability to distinguish right from left; dominant parietal (Gerstmann syndrome).
simple: Trouble telling right from left. Seen with damage to a specific part of the brain's left parietal lobe, as part of a group of symptoms called Gerstmann syndrome.

name: Rooting Reflex
formal: Head turns toward and mouth opens to a touch at the corner of the mouth; primitive/frontal release sign.
simple: Touching the corner of a baby's mouth makes the head turn toward the touch and the mouth open, a normal reflex in infants that, in adults, signals frontal brain dysfunction.

name: Self-Mutilation
formal: Self-injurious behaviour; Lesch-Nyhan, neuroacanthocytosis, insensitivity to pain, Tourette.
simple: Behavior where a person injures their own body. Seen in certain genetic conditions, disorders that reduce pain sensation, or Tourette syndrome.

name: Sighing
formal: Frequent sighing respiration; MSA, anxiety.
simple: Breathing out with frequent, deep sighs. Can occur in multiple system atrophy (a Parkinson's-like disease) or simply from anxiety.

name: Signe de Rideau
formal: Curtain sign: posterior pharyngeal wall moves toward the intact side on phonation; unilateral IX/X palsy.
simple: When the patient says "ah," the back wall of the throat pulls sideways toward the healthy side, like a curtain being drawn. Shows one-sided weakness of the throat nerves.

name: Simian Hand
formal: Flattened "ape hand" from thenar wasting (thumb in plane of the palm); median nerve/C8–T1 lesions.
simple: The hand looks flattened like an "ape hand," with the thumb lying in the same plane as the palm, from wasting of the thumb's base muscles. Comes from damage to the median nerve or a nearby part of the spinal cord.

name: Smile-Wink Phenomenon
formal: Narrowing of the palpebral fissure worsened by smiling; contralateral lenticulocapsular infarct.
simple: One eye narrows more than usual specifically when the person smiles. Linked to a stroke deep in the opposite side of the brain.

name: Snoring
formal: Sleep-disordered breathing; stridor in MSA.
simple: Loud breathing sounds during sleep from a partly blocked airway; if paired with a harsh, high-pitched sound (stridor), it can be a warning sign in multiple system atrophy.

name: Spasmus Nutans
formal: Infantile triad of head nodding, pendular nystagmus and head tilt; benign or chiasmal/hypothalamic glioma.
simple: In infants, a combination of head nodding, small back-and-forth eye movements, and head tilting. Usually harmless, but occasionally linked to a brain tumor near the visual pathway.

name: Split hand
formal: Thenar and first dorsal interosseous wasted more than hypothenar; characteristic of ALS.
simple: In ALS (a disease that damages nerve cells controlling muscles), the muscles at the base of the thumb waste away more than the muscles on the other side of the palm, an early and distinctive pattern.

name: Striatal Toe
formal: Tonic spontaneous extension of the great toe; parkinsonism/dystonia (not a Babinski sign).
simple: The big toe stays stuck pointing upward on its own, not because of a reflex test, but as an ongoing posture. Seen in Parkinson's-type disorders or dystonia, and should not be confused with a positive Babinski reflex.

name: Synesthesia
formal: Stimulation of one sense evokes perception in another (e.g. colour with sounds).
simple: Stimulating one sense triggers a perception in another, such as "seeing" colors when hearing sounds.

name: Tinnitus
formal: Ringing or noise in the ears; cochlear, VIII nerve (vestibular schwannoma) or vascular (pulsatile) causes.
simple: Ringing or other noise heard in the ears without an outside source. Can come from the inner ear, the hearing nerve (including from a growth called vestibular schwannoma), or abnormal blood flow.

name: Vegetative States
formal: Wakefulness without awareness (eyes open, sleep–wake cycles) after severe brain injury.
simple: A condition of being awake, with normal sleep and wake cycles and open eyes, but without any awareness of self or surroundings, following severe brain injury.

name: Waiter’s Tip Posture
formal: Arm adducted and internally rotated with pronated forearm and flexed wrist; upper trunk (C5–C6, Erb) palsy.
simple: The arm hangs with the shoulder turned inward, the forearm rotated so the palm faces backward, and the wrist bent, resembling a waiter asking for a tip. Comes from an injury to the upper nerves that supply the arm, near the shoulder.

name: Wartenberg’s Swing Test
formal: Reduced arm swing / damping of passive leg swing when the legs dangle; assesses rigidity (parkinsonism).
simple: When the legs are allowed to dangle and swing freely, the swinging is reduced or dampened. Used to detect muscle stiffness from Parkinsonism.

name: Wrestler’s Sign
formal: Excessive effort in irrelevant muscles with grunting during strength testing; functional weakness.
simple: During a strength test, the person visibly strains many unrelated muscles and grunts with effort, a clue that the weakness being tested is not from a genuine nerve or brain problem.

name: Wrist Drop
formal: Weak wrist and finger extension; radial nerve palsy (spiral groove), C7 root, posterior interosseous nerve.
simple: Weakness in lifting the wrist and fingers upward. Caused by damage to the radial nerve in the arm, a pinched nerve root in the neck (C7), or a related nerve further down the arm.

name: Babinski Sign (Extensor Plantar Response)
formal: Dorsiflexion of the great toe, often with fanning of the other toes, when the lateral sole is stroked; indicates dysfunction of the corticospinal tract (normal in infants under about 1 year).
simple: When the outer edge of the sole is scratched, the big toe goes up instead of curling down — a sign that the brain or spinal cord pathway for movement is damaged.
th: ขูดฝ่าเท้าด้านนอกแล้วนิ้วโป้งกระดกขึ้น — บ่งชี้ทางเดินประสาทสั่งการจากสมอง (UMN) เสียหาย
exam: Patient supine, leg relaxed. With a blunt point, stroke the lateral sole slowly from heel toward the little toe, then curve medially across the metatarsal heads. Watch the first movement of the great toe.
pos: Initial slow, sustained great-toe extension (± toe fanning, hip/knee flexion) = upper motor neuron lesion anywhere from cortex to spinal cord. A withdrawal of the whole foot or an equivocal response is not positive.
aN: extensor plantar response | babinski sign | babinski | upgoing plantar | extensor plantar | plantar response | upgoing te | babinski reflex

det.mechanism: The great-toe extension is part of a primitive flexion-withdrawal synergy in which extensor hallucis longus behaves as a 'shortening' muscle of the leg. In infancy and after corticospinal damage, descending control that normally converts this into plantar flexion is absent, so the withdrawal pattern re-emerges. The response therefore reflects pyramidal tract dysfunction rather than a specific site along it.
det.technique: Keep the leg relaxed and warm, and use a firm but not painful blunt object. Stroke the outer border of the sole slowly, curving across the ball of the foot, and watch only the first movement of the hallux. Alternative stimuli (Chaddock on the lateral foot, Oppenheim down the shin) can confirm an equivocal result. Errors include painful stimuli provoking withdrawal, and mistaking voluntary toe lifting in ticklish patients.
det.interpretation: A clear upgoing toe signals corticospinal involvement anywhere from motor cortex to spinal cord; it may be absent in early or mild lesions, so a flexor response does not exclude UMN disease. It can transiently appear after seizures, in deep sleep, coma or hypoglycaemia. A lesion of the peroneal nerve or L5 root can abolish the response altogether (mute plantar). Interobserver agreement is only moderate, so interpret alongside tone, reflexes and weakness pattern.
pearls: Judge the first movement of the big toe only.
An absent response is not the same as a flexor response.
Normal until roughly 12 months of age.
det.thd: Babinski เกิดจากทางเดินประสาท corticospinal เสียทำให้ปฏิกิริยาถอนเท้าแบบดั้งเดิมกลับมา นิ้วโป้งจึงกระดกขึ้น ให้ขูดฝ่าเท้าด้านนอกช้า ๆ ด้วยของทู่และดูการเคลื่อนไหวแรกของนิ้วโป้ง พบได้ในรอยโรค UMN ทุกระดับตั้งแต่สมองถึงไขสันหลัง แต่ผลลบไม่ตัดโรคออก และอาจพบชั่วคราวหลังชัก หมดสติ หรือน้ำตาลต่ำ

name: Hoffmann Sign
formal: Reflex flexion of the thumb and index finger when the distal phalanx of the middle finger is flicked; suggests corticospinal tract dysfunction above C5–C6 when asymmetric or accompanied by other UMN signs.
simple: Flicking the tip of the middle finger makes the thumb and index finger twitch inward — a clue to a problem in the spinal cord in the neck or the brain.
th: ดีดปลายนิ้วกลางแล้วนิ้วโป้งกับนิ้วชี้งอเข้าหากัน — บ่งชี้รอยโรค UMN ระดับคอขึ้นไป
exam: Support the patient's relaxed hand with the wrist slightly extended. Hold the middle finger and flick its nail downward with your thumb so the distal phalanx snaps into extension.
pos: Flexion-adduction of thumb and index finger. Bilateral and symmetric can be a normal brisk-reflex variant; unilateral or with other UMN signs suggests cervical myelopathy or a brain lesion.
aN: hoffmann | hoffman sign | finger flexor reflex

det.mechanism: Flicking the distal phalanx produces a sudden stretch of the deep finger flexors, a monosynaptic stretch reflex at roughly C7–T1. When descending inhibition is lost, the reflex spreads so the thumb and index finger flex. It is essentially a finger-flexor jerk made visible by hyperexcitability.
det.technique: Relax the patient's hand, wrist slightly extended and fingers loosely flexed. Hold the middle finger at the middle phalanx and flick the nail sharply downward or upward. Repeat several times on both sides; neck flexion may increase yield in subtle cervical myelopathy (dynamic Hoffmann).
det.interpretation: Asymmetric or strong responses with other UMN signs suggest a lesion above C5–C6, commonly cervical spondylotic myelopathy, MS or ALS. Symmetric mild responses occur in some healthy people with brisk reflexes or anxiety and are not pathological alone. Sensitivity for cervical cord compression is modest, so a negative test does not exclude myelopathy.
pearls: Unilateral Hoffmann matters more than symmetric bilateral Hoffmann.
Combine with inverted supinator jerk and gait assessment in suspected myelopathy.
det.thd: Hoffmann คือรีเฟล็กซ์ยืดของกล้ามเนื้องอนิ้วที่ไวเกินเมื่อขาดการยับยั้งจากสมอง ให้ดีดปลายเล็บนิ้วกลางแล้วดูนิ้วโป้งกับนิ้วชี้งอ ถ้าเป็นข้างเดียวหรือร่วมกับอาการ UMN อื่นนึกถึงรอยโรคไขสันหลังส่วนคอหรือสมอง แต่ถ้าเป็นสองข้างเท่ากันเล็กน้อยอาจเป็นปกติในคนที่รีเฟล็กซ์ไว

name: Pronator Drift
formal: With arms outstretched, palms up and eyes closed, the weak arm pronates and drifts downward; a sensitive sign of mild corticospinal weakness.
simple: Holding both arms straight out with palms up and eyes shut, a weak arm slowly turns inward and sinks — a sensitive test for mild weakness from the brain.
th: เหยียดแขนสองข้างหงายมือ หลับตา แขนข้างที่อ่อนแรงจะคว่ำและตกลง — บ่งชี้ UMN weakness เล็กน้อย
exam: Ask the patient to hold both arms straight forward, palms facing the ceiling, eyes closed, for 20–30 seconds. Optionally tap the arms downward.
pos: Pronation and downward drift = contralateral UMN lesion. Upward/outward drift without pronation suggests proprioceptive loss (parietal) or cerebellar disorder; drift without pronation can be functional.
aN: pronator drift | barre sign | arm drift | barre test

det.mechanism: Corticospinal weakness preferentially affects antigravity extensors and supinators of the arm, so the stronger pronators and flexors take over when the arm is held supinated. The limb therefore turns palm-down and sinks. Without vision, patients cannot correct position, making mild weakness evident.
det.technique: Ask the patient to hold both arms forward at shoulder height, palms up, fingers together, eyes closed, for at least 20–30 seconds. Observe for pronation, elbow flexion and downward drift, and compare sides. A gentle downward tap can unmask subtle weakness; check for finger spreading or rolling of the forearms as additional subtle signs.
det.interpretation: Pronation with downward drift points to a contralateral UMN lesion and is more sensitive than formal power testing for mild weakness. Upward or lateral wandering without pronation suggests loss of position sense (parietal lesion — pseudoathetosis) or cerebellar disease. Drift without pronation, or variable effort, raises the possibility of functional weakness.
pearls: Pronation is the key component, not just downward drift.
Eyes must be closed to remove visual correction.
det.thd: Pronator drift เกิดเพราะ UMN weakness ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อเหยียดและหงายแขนอ่อนกว่ากล้ามเนื้อคว่ำและงอ ให้ผู้ป่วยเหยียดแขนหงายมือหลับตา 20–30 วินาที ถ้าแขนคว่ำและตกลงบ่งชี้รอยโรคฝั่งตรงข้ามและไวกว่าการตรวจกำลังปกติ ถ้าแขนลอยขึ้นหรือออกด้านข้างโดยไม่คว่ำ นึกถึงปัญหา proprioception หรือสมองน้อย

name: Romberg Sign
formal: Loss of balance when standing with feet together and eyes closed that was absent with eyes open; indicates impaired proprioception (sensory ataxia) rather than cerebellar ataxia.
simple: The patient can stand with feet together while looking, but sways or falls when the eyes are closed — showing they rely on vision because position sense from the legs is lost.
th: ยืนเท้าชิดลืมตาได้ แต่หลับตาแล้วเซ/ล้ม — บ่งชี้การรับรู้ตำแหน่งข้อ (proprioception) เสีย ไม่ใช่โรคสมองน้อย
exam: Patient stands with feet together, arms by the sides. First eyes open, then eyes closed for up to 60 s. Stand close to prevent falls.
pos: Positive only if stable with eyes open and markedly unstable with eyes closed: dorsal column or large-fibre neuropathy (B12 deficiency, tabes, CIDP, sensory neuronopathy). Cerebellar patients are unsteady even with eyes open.
aN: romberg | romberg test | rombergism | sensory ataxia test

det.mechanism: Upright balance depends on three inputs: vision, vestibular function and joint position sense from the legs. If proprioception is lost, the patient compensates with vision; closing the eyes removes the last reliable input, and sway increases sharply. Cerebellar ataxia does not depend on vision in the same way, so patients are unsteady regardless.
det.technique: Have the patient stand with feet together, arms by the sides or crossed, first with eyes open until steady, then with eyes closed for up to a minute. Stand close and be ready to catch. A sharpened (tandem) Romberg increases sensitivity in mild cases but is harder for older people. Do not count mild sway as positive.
det.interpretation: A positive test (stable with eyes open, falls or steps with eyes closed) indicates sensory ataxia from dorsal column or large-fibre peripheral disease, such as B12 deficiency, tabes, CIDP or ganglionopathy. Bilateral vestibular loss can also produce a positive Romberg. Inability to stand with feet together even with eyes open suggests cerebellar or other disease, and the test is then not interpretable. Exaggerated sway that improves with distraction suggests a functional cause.
pearls: Romberg tests proprioception, not cerebellar function.
Must be stable with eyes open for the test to be valid.
det.thd: Romberg เป็นการทดสอบ proprioception เมื่อการรับรู้ตำแหน่งข้อจากขาเสียผู้ป่วยจะอาศัยสายตาแทน พอหลับตาจึงเซหรือล้ม ให้ยืนเท้าชิดลืมตาจนนิ่งแล้วหลับตาโดยผู้ตรวจยืนใกล้ ผลบวกบ่งชี้ dorsal column หรือเส้นประสาทใยใหญ่เสีย (B12 ต่ำ, tabes, CIDP) ส่วนผู้ป่วยสมองน้อยจะเซแม้ลืมตา

name: Clonus
formal: Rhythmic involuntary muscle contractions provoked by sudden sustained stretch, most often at the ankle; more than a few beats indicates upper motor neuron hyperexcitability.
simple: When the foot is quickly pushed up and held, it keeps bouncing up and down by itself — a sign of an overactive reflex from brain or spinal cord damage.
th: ดันข้อเท้าขึ้นเร็ว ๆ แล้วค้างไว้ เท้ากระตุกเป็นจังหวะต่อเนื่อง — บ่งชี้ UMN lesion
exam: With the knee slightly flexed and supported, briskly dorsiflex the foot and hold gentle pressure.
pos: Sustained (>3–5 beats) = UMN lesion. A few unsustained beats may be normal with anxiety or brisk reflexes; serotonin toxicity gives inducible clonus too.
aN: ankle clonus | sustained clonus | patellar clonus

det.mechanism: Clonus is a self-sustaining oscillation in which each stretch evokes a reflex contraction that relaxes and re-stretches the muscle, triggering the next beat. It requires hyperexcitable stretch reflex circuits after loss of descending inhibition, and the beat frequency (around 5–7 Hz at the ankle) depends on the reflex loop time. It is the extreme end of hyperreflexia.
det.technique: Support the leg with the knee slightly flexed and the muscles relaxed. Dorsiflex the ankle briskly and maintain moderate upward pressure on the sole; count the beats. Patellar clonus is elicited by a sharp downward push of the patella with the knee extended. Tense, cold or poorly positioned limbs give false negatives.
det.interpretation: Sustained clonus (more than a few beats continuing while stretch is held) indicates an UMN lesion. A short unsustained run of beats can occur in anxious or healthy people, especially if symmetrical. Asymmetry is more significant than amplitude. Inducible and ocular clonus with hyperthermia and agitation suggest serotonin toxicity.
pearls: Count and record the number of beats.
Symmetrical non-sustained clonus may be normal.
det.thd: Clonus เกิดจากรีเฟล็กซ์ยืดที่ไวมากจนกระตุกต่อเนื่องเป็นรอบ ๆ เมื่อขาดการยับยั้งจากสมอง ตรวจโดยงอเข่าเล็กน้อยแล้วดันข้อเท้าขึ้นเร็ว ๆ ค้างไว้และนับจำนวนครั้ง ถ้ากระตุกต่อเนื่องมากกว่า 3–5 ครั้งบ่งชี้รอยโรค UMN แต่ถ้ากระตุกไม่กี่ครั้งสองข้างเท่ากันอาจเป็นปกติ และพบใน serotonin toxicity ได้

name: Kernig Sign
formal: Resistance or pain on extending the knee with the hip flexed to 90°, reflecting meningeal irritation.
simple: With the hip bent, straightening the knee causes pain and resistance in the back — a sign of inflamed coverings of the brain and spine.
th: งอสะโพก 90° แล้วเหยียดเข่าไม่ได้เพราะปวด — บ่งชี้เยื่อหุ้มสมองระคายเคือง
exam: Patient supine. Flex hip and knee to 90°, then try to extend the knee.
pos: Pain/resistance limiting extension = meningeal irritation (meningitis, SAH). Low sensitivity — a negative test does not exclude meningitis.

det.mechanism: Extending the knee while the hip is flexed stretches the sciatic nerve and lumbosacral roots through the subarachnoid space. If the meninges and roots are inflamed or irritated by blood, this stretch is painful, so the hamstrings contract protectively to limit extension.
det.technique: With the patient supine, flex the hip and knee to 90 degrees, then slowly extend the knee. Positive when pain in the back or posterior thigh and resistance prevent extension beyond about 135 degrees. Perform bilaterally; unilateral resistance suggests a root problem rather than meningitis.
det.interpretation: Specificity for meningitis is relatively high, but sensitivity is low (often well under 20% in adult series), so a negative result must never delay lumbar puncture when meningitis is suspected. Signs may be absent in infants, the elderly, immunosuppressed or comatose patients. Lumbar disc disease and hamstring tightness can mimic a positive test.
pearls: Low sensitivity — do not use to rule out meningitis.
Bilateral finding favours meningeal irritation; unilateral suggests radiculopathy.
det.thd: Kernig sign เกิดจากการเหยียดเข่าขณะงอสะโพกทำให้รากประสาทและเยื่อหุ้มที่อักเสบถูกยืด จึงปวดและเหยียดไม่ได้ ตรวจโดยงอสะโพกและเข่า 90 องศาแล้วค่อย ๆ เหยียดเข่า ความไวต่ำมาก ผลลบจึงไม่ตัดเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ ถ้าสงสัยยังต้องเจาะหลังหรือให้ยาตามข้อบ่งชี้

name: Brudzinski Neck Sign
formal: Involuntary flexion of hips and knees when the neck is passively flexed, indicating meningeal irritation.
simple: Bending the patient's head forward makes the knees and hips bend by themselves — a sign of meningitis or bleeding around the brain.
th: ก้มคอผู้ป่วยแล้วสะโพกเข่างอเอง — บ่งชี้เยื่อหุ้มสมองระคายเคือง
exam: Patient supine; place a hand behind the head and flex the neck toward the chest.
pos: Reflex hip/knee flexion = meningeal irritation; specific but insensitive.

det.mechanism: Neck flexion pulls the spinal cord and its coverings upward, placing tension on inflamed meninges and roots. The patient reflexively flexes the hips and knees to slacken this tension and reduce pain.
det.technique: With the patient supine and relaxed, place one hand under the occiput and flex the neck forward while the other hand rests on the chest to stop the trunk rising. Watch the hips and knees for spontaneous flexion. Avoid if cervical spine injury is possible.
det.interpretation: A positive response supports meningeal irritation from infection or subarachnoid blood, with reasonable specificity but low sensitivity. It is not a reliable discriminator in the very young or old. Neck flexion resistance alone may come from cervical spondylosis or parkinsonian rigidity rather than meningitis.
pearls: Like Kernig, a negative result does not exclude meningitis.
Other Brudzinski variants (contralateral leg) exist but are rarely used.
det.thd: Brudzinski sign คือเมื่อก้มคอผู้ป่วยแล้วสะโพกและเข่างอเองเพื่อลดแรงดึงเยื่อหุ้มที่อักเสบ ตรวจในท่านอนหงายโดยประคองท้ายทอยแล้วก้มคอ ผลบวกสนับสนุนเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบหรือเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง แต่ความไวต่ำ ผลลบไม่ตัดโรค

name: Neck Stiffness
formal: Resistance to passive neck flexion with preserved rotation, a feature of meningeal irritation; global resistance in all directions suggests cervical spine disease or parkinsonian rigidity instead.
simple: The chin cannot be brought down to the chest because of pain and stiffness, though turning the head side to side is fine — typical of meningitis or bleeding.
th: คอแข็ง ก้มคอไม่ได้แต่หันซ้ายขวาได้ — บ่งชี้เยื่อหุ้มสมองระคายเคือง
exam: Patient lying flat; gently lift the head to flex the neck, then test rotation.
pos: Resistance to flexion only = meningeal irritation; may be absent in coma, infants, the elderly and early disease.
aN: nuchal rigidity | meningism | neck rigidity | meningismus

det.mechanism: Inflammation or blood in the subarachnoid space irritates the meninges and nerve roots; neck flexion stretches these structures, triggering protective spasm of the posterior neck muscles. Rotation stretches the meninges much less, so it is relatively preserved, unlike in bony or extrapyramidal stiffness.
det.technique: With the patient lying flat and the head on your hands, gently lift the head to bring the chin toward the chest, then rotate side to side. Resistance to flexion with free rotation is the characteristic pattern. The jolt accentuation test (worsening headache with rapid horizontal head turning) may be added in alert patients.
det.interpretation: Neck stiffness supports meningitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage but has limited sensitivity; it may be absent early, in deep coma, in infants and in older or immunocompromised patients. Resistance in all directions suggests cervical spondylosis, parkinsonism or neck pain. Tonsillar herniation can also cause neck stiffness, so fundoscopy and imaging may be needed before lumbar puncture when indicated.
pearls: Flexion-only stiffness = meningeal; all directions = mechanical or rigidity.
Absence does not exclude meningitis in coma or the elderly.
det.thd: คอแข็งเกิดจากเยื่อหุ้มสมองระคายเคืองจากการอักเสบหรือเลือด ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อคอหดเกร็งเมื่อก้มคอ แต่หันซ้ายขวาได้ปกติ ตรวจโดยยกศีรษะผู้ป่วยให้คางชิดอกแล้วลองหมุนคอ ถ้าแข็งทุกทิศทางนึกถึงโรคกระดูกคอหรือ rigidity มากกว่า ความไวไม่สูงโดยเฉพาะในผู้สูงอายุหรือผู้ป่วยหมดสติ

name: Fatigable Ptosis
formal: Ptosis that worsens with sustained upgaze and improves with rest or cooling; characteristic of neuromuscular junction transmission failure.
simple: The eyelid droops more and more when the person looks up for a while, and gets better after rest or an ice pack — typical of myasthenia gravis.
th: หนังตาตกที่มากขึ้นเมื่อมองขึ้นนาน ๆ ดีขึ้นเมื่อพักหรือประคบเย็น — นึกถึง myasthenia gravis
exam: Ask the patient to look up at your finger without blinking for 60 seconds; observe the lid margin and note new diplopia. Compare after an ice pack for 2 minutes.
pos: Progressive lid descent with sustained upgaze, improvement with ice/rest; pupils normal = neuromuscular junction disease (MG). Look for Cogan lid twitch and curtain sign.
aN: fatigable ptosis | ptosis fatigable | sustained upgaze test | simpson test | droopy eyelid

det.mechanism: In myasthenia gravis, fewer functional acetylcholine receptors reduce the safety margin of neuromuscular transmission. With sustained contraction, acetylcholine release per impulse falls, and more fibres fail to reach threshold, so the levator weakens progressively. Cold slows acetylcholinesterase and improves transmission, explaining the ice pack effect.
det.technique: Ask the patient to keep looking up at a target held above eye level for about one minute without blinking. Measure or observe the lid margin relative to the pupil at the start and end, and ask about new double vision. Check for Cogan lid twitch (overshoot of the lid on returning from downgaze) and enhanced ptosis (the opposite lid falls when the more ptotic lid is lifted).
det.interpretation: Progressive ptosis with sustained upgaze, normal pupils and variable ophthalmoparesis strongly suggests neuromuscular junction disease, chiefly MG. It may also occur in LEMS, botulism and some congenital myasthenic syndromes. Third nerve palsy, Horner syndrome and aponeurotic ptosis are not fatigable, though apparent fatigue can occur in mechanical ptosis from brow strain.
pearls: Pupils are spared in MG — pupil involvement suggests third nerve or botulism.
Look for curtain sign (enhanced ptosis) by lifting the more ptotic lid.
det.thd: หนังตาตกแบบ fatigable เกิดเพราะใน myasthenia gravis จุดเชื่อมประสาท-กล้ามเนื้อมีตัวรับ acetylcholine น้อยลง เมื่อใช้กล้ามเนื้อต่อเนื่องจึงล้า ตรวจโดยให้มองขึ้นค้างประมาณ 1 นาทีและดูว่าหนังตาตกมากขึ้นหรือมีภาพซ้อน รูม่านตาปกติ ร่วมกับ Cogan lid twitch และ curtain sign บ่งชี้โรค NMJ

name: Horner Syndrome
formal: Ipsilateral mild ptosis, miosis with dilation lag and variable facial anhidrosis from interruption of the oculosympathetic pathway (hypothalamus → brainstem → cord → sympathetic chain → carotid plexus).
simple: A small pupil, slightly droopy eyelid and sometimes less sweating on one side of the face, caused by damage to the nerve pathway that runs from the brain down the neck and back up to the eye.
th: หนังตาตกเล็กน้อย รูม่านตาเล็ก เหงื่อออกน้อยข้างเดียวกัน — เส้นทางประสาท sympathetic ไปตาเสียหาย
exam: Compare pupils in bright and dim light (anisocoria greater in the dark), look for dilation lag, upper and lower lid ptosis, and check facial sweating.
pos: Central (stroke/demyelination, with other brainstem signs), preganglionic (lung apex, neck trauma) or postganglionic (carotid dissection, cluster headache). Painful acute Horner = carotid dissection until proven otherwise.
aN: horner | horner syndrome | oculosympathetic palsy | bernard horner

det.mechanism: The oculosympathetic pathway is a three-neuron chain: from the hypothalamus through the lateral brainstem to the C8–T2 cord (first order), over the lung apex to the superior cervical ganglion (second order), then along the internal carotid artery into the cavernous sinus and orbit (third order). Interruption anywhere weakens the pupil dilator and Müller's muscle, giving miosis and mild ptosis, with anhidrosis depending on the level.
det.technique: Examine pupils in bright and then dim light; anisocoria that increases in darkness with slow re-dilation of the small pupil (dilation lag) supports Horner. Look for slight upper lid ptosis and lower lid elevation (upside-down ptosis). Pharmacological testing with apraclonidine (reversal of anisocoria) or cocaine confirms the diagnosis; hydroxyamphetamine helps localise third-order lesions.
det.interpretation: Associated features localise the lesion: brainstem signs (lateral medullary syndrome), myelopathy, arm pain or hand wasting (Pancoast tumour, lower trunk plexopathy), or neck pain and headache (carotid dissection). Anhidrosis of the whole half body or face suggests central or preganglionic lesions; postganglionic lesions spare most facial sweating. Congenital Horner causes iris heterochromia. Physiological anisocoria lacks ptosis and dilation lag.
pearls: Acute painful Horner = carotid dissection until imaging says otherwise.
Anisocoria worse in the dark points to the small pupil as abnormal.
Look for a Pancoast tumour in smokers with shoulder pain and Horner.
det.thd: Horner syndrome เกิดจากเส้นทางประสาท sympathetic ไปตา 3 ช่วง (สมอง-ไขสันหลัง, ยอดปอด-คอ, ตามหลอดเลือด carotid) ถูกขัดขวาง ทำให้รูม่านตาเล็ก หนังตาตกเล็กน้อย และอาจเหงื่อออกน้อย ตรวจในที่มืดจะเห็นรูม่านตาต่างกันมากขึ้นและขยายช้า อาการร่วมช่วยบอกตำแหน่ง ถ้าเกิดฉับพลันร่วมกับปวดคอ/ปวดหัวต้องคิดถึง carotid dissection ก่อน

name: Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD)
formal: Paradoxical dilation of both pupils when a light is swung from the normal to the affected eye, indicating asymmetric afferent (optic nerve or extensive retinal) dysfunction.
simple: When a torch swings from one eye to the other, both pupils widen when the light reaches the damaged eye — showing that eye's optic nerve passes less light signal.
th: ส่องไฟสลับตา เมื่อไฟมาที่ตาข้างผิดปกติรูม่านตาทั้งสองขยาย — บ่งชี้เส้นประสาทตาข้างนั้นเสีย
exam: In a dim room, swing a bright light briskly between the eyes, pausing 2–3 seconds on each.
pos: Dilation on illumination of one eye = afferent defect in that eye (optic neuritis, ischaemic optic neuropathy, compression). Cataract does not cause RAPD.
aN: rapd | relative afferent pupillary defect | marcus gunn pupil | swinging flashlight test | afferent pupillary defect

det.mechanism: Light entering either eye drives both pupils equally via the pretectal nuclei and bilateral Edinger–Westphal connections. If one optic nerve transmits less signal, both pupils constrict less when that eye is lit than when the healthy eye is lit. Swinging the light quickly exposes this imbalance as dilation when the beam moves to the affected side.
det.technique: Dim the room and have the patient fixate a distant target. Swing a bright torch from one eye to the other, holding about 2–3 seconds on each, and watch the initial pupil response of the eye being illuminated. Repeat several times; neutral density filters can grade the defect. If one pupil is fixed or unreactive, observe the other pupil (reverse RAPD).
det.interpretation: An RAPD indicates asymmetric afferent damage — optic neuropathy (optic neuritis, ischaemic, compressive, glaucoma) or extensive retinal disease such as large detachment. Media opacities like cataract and refractive error do not cause it, and amblyopia only rarely gives a mild defect. Symmetric bilateral optic neuropathy may produce no RAPD. A small RAPD can occur with optic tract lesions in the eye with the temporal field loss.
pearls: Cataract does not cause RAPD — look for nerve or retina.
Bilateral equal disease may show no RAPD.
det.thd: RAPD เกิดเพราะเส้นประสาทตาข้างหนึ่งส่งสัญญาณแสงได้น้อยกว่า เมื่อส่องไฟสลับจากตาปกติไปตาที่ผิดปกติ รูม่านตาทั้งสองจึงขยายแทนที่จะหด ตรวจในห้องมืดโดยส่องไฟสลับช้า ๆ ข้างละ 2–3 วินาที ผลบวกบ่งชี้โรคเส้นประสาทตาหรือจอประสาทตาเสียกว้าง แต่ต้อกระจกไม่ทำให้เกิด RAPD

name: Dysdiadochokinesia
formal: Impaired performance of rapid alternating movements (e.g. pronation–supination), with irregular rhythm and amplitude; a sign of ipsilateral cerebellar hemisphere dysfunction.
simple: Difficulty quickly flipping the hand back and forth — the movements become clumsy and uneven, pointing to a problem in the cerebellum on the same side.
th: พลิกมือคว่ำหงายเร็ว ๆ ไม่สม่ำเสมอ — บ่งชี้สมองน้อยข้างเดียวกันผิดปกติ
exam: Ask the patient to tap the palm and back of one hand alternately on the other palm or thigh as fast as possible; compare sides.
pos: Irregular rhythm/force = ipsilateral cerebellar lesion. Slow but rhythmic with decrement suggests parkinsonism; slow due to weakness suggests UMN.

det.mechanism: Rapid alternating movements require precise timing of agonist cessation and antagonist onset. The cerebellum predicts and coordinates these switches; when it is damaged, timing and force become variable, so movements lose rhythm and amplitude consistency. Cerebellar hemispheres control the ipsilateral limbs.
det.technique: Ask the patient to pat one hand on the other palm or thigh, alternating palm and back, as fast and regularly as possible, and listen as well as look; repeat with the other hand. In the legs, ask for rapid foot tapping. Compare sides and note slowing versus irregularity, since weakness or rigidity slow movements without causing dysrhythmia.
det.interpretation: Irregular rhythm, force and range indicate ipsilateral cerebellar or cerebellar pathway dysfunction, as in MS, stroke, alcohol-related or degenerative ataxia. Progressive slowing and decreasing amplitude (decrement) suggest parkinsonism. Pure slowness with otherwise smooth rhythm is seen with UMN weakness. The non-dominant hand is normally slightly slower.
pearls: Listen to the rhythm — the irregular sound is often more obvious than the look.
Decrement = parkinsonism; dysrhythmia = cerebellum.
